nara_8nosu_hachinosu_3.gf_detail: No gluten-free claim is published. It is a soup curry rather than a thick wheat-roux curry, but there is no documented information on whether the spice blend, soup, or sides are wheat-free, and no cross-contamination details. A celiac diner would need to ask directly and should not assume it is safe.
nara_8nosu_hachinosu_3.vegan_detail: A vegetable-only curry exists (about ¥880-¥950), but the soup base is made with chicken-bone and dried-fish (niboshi) dashi, and the curries contain honey, so even the vegetable option is not vegan or strictly vegetarian. Not a vegan destination.
nara_8nosu_hachinosu_3.hours_raw: Sources conflict. Tabelog: 11:30-15:00 and 17:30-20:00, closed Thursday. Official jimdo site: lunch 11:30-15:00 (LO 14:30), dinner 17:30-20:00 (LO 19:30), closed Fridays, additional closures via Instagram, closes when sold out. Narakko: weekdays 11:00-15:00 & 17:00-20:00, weekends/holidays 11:00-17:00, closed Tuesdays and 2nd & 4th Wednesdays.
nara_8nosu_hachinosu_3.notes: 8nosu is a small spice-curry-and-honey shop tucked into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's Naramachi district, a short walk south of Sarusawa Pond and Kofuku-ji Temple. chef_bio.background: 8nosu is a small spice-curry-and-honey shop tucked into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's Naramachi district, a short walk south of Sarusawa Pond and Kofuku-ji Temple. It is run by a certified yakuzen (medicinal-herb cooking) coordinator who built the menu around the idea of food as everyday wellness.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built on the motto 食べて元気になる - eat and become well - applying medicinal-herb principles so a casual curry lunch doubles as nourishment.
chef_bio.specialty: Stone-bowl soup curry built from about 20 spices and seasonal medicinal-herb vegetables. Diners choose a base (vegetable-only, soft chicken, or slow-braised pork), a soup style (original, coconut, or shrimp), and a spice level. House drinks include lassi, masala chai, and a honey-lemon squash made with domestic lemons and pure honey from Nara's Uda area (Ito-yu Beekeeping), which is also sold by the jar.

anecdotes.text: Because honey features in the shop's menu and products, it notes that honey items are not suitable for infants under one year old.
The honey served and sold is pure domestic honey from Ito-yu Beekeeping in the Uda area of Nara Prefecture.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: narakko.jp confirms a薬膳 (yakuzen) coordinator runs this 食べて元気になる薬膳カレー shop serving stone-bowl soup curry from ~20 spices with vegetable/chicken/pork bases, and that it uses and sells pure Ito-yu 国産はちみつ honey from Nara's Uda area.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The soup base for all curries, including the vegetable-only option, is made with chicken-bone and dried-fish (niboshi) dashi, so vegetable dishes share an animal-derived broth.
Curries contain honey.

positives.text: A vegetable-only medicinal-herb soup curry is offered as a standing menu choice (though it is not vegan due to the broth and honey).

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, friendly Naramachi cafe used to tourists and international visitors; menu is build-your-own (base, soup, spice level, rice), so a few words of Japanese or pointing will go a long way.

nara_main_dining_room_mikasa__2.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free program. Classic French cuisine relies on flour-thickened sauces, bread, and pastry, and the kitchen states all dishes are prepared in the same kitchen so cross-contamination is possible. The hotel does offer allergy accommodation if you notify them well in advance of your reservation, so a celiac or gluten-avoidant diner should call ahead (0742-24-3044) and discuss specific needs, but this is not a celiac-safe environment by default.
nara_main_dining_room_mikasa__2.vegan_detail: The restaurant advertises ovo-lacto vegetarian course options (which include eggs and dairy, so not vegan) and builds menus around seasonal Yamato vegetables and local Nara produce. There is no documented fully vegan menu; French cooking here uses butter, cream, dairy and likely meat/fish stocks. Strict vegans should contact the restaurant in advance to ask what can be prepared, but should not assume vegan dishes are available off the standard menu.
nara_main_dining_room_mikasa__2.notes: The main dining room of the Nara Hotel, which opened in 1909 in the Takabatake area beside Nara Park. The dining room has served guests since the hotel's founding and has hosted dignitaries and celebrities from Japan and abroad in a preserved Meiji–Taisho era setting.

chef_bio.origin: Nara (奈良市高畑町), within the historic Nara Hotel
chef_bio.background: The main dining room of the Nara Hotel, which opened in 1909 in the Takabatake area beside Nara Park. The dining room has served guests since the hotel's founding and has hosted dignitaries and celebrities from Japan and abroad in a preserved Meiji–Taisho era setting.
chef_bio.philosophy: The head chef describes the goal as French cuisine that brings smiles and emotion befitting the tradition and history of the Nara Hotel (伝統と歴史を培った奈良ホテルに相応しい笑顔と感動を与えるフランス料理).
chef_bio.specialty: Traditional French cuisine built on seasonal Yamato vegetables and local Nara ingredients, with recipes handed down through successive head chefs since the hotel opened.

anecdotes.text: The dining room has been part of the Nara Hotel since its 1909 founding and carries on traditional French cuisine inherited from successive head chefs, served in a preserved Meiji–Taisho-era room.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Nara Hotel site names head chef 乾 陽介 (Yosuke Inui), states the Main Dining Room 'Mikasa' has served since the hotel's 1909 opening, carries French cuisine inherited from successive head chefs, uses 大和野菜 Yamato vegetables, and quotes the chef's aim of 笑顔と感動 French cuisine befitting the hotel's tradition.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All dishes are prepared in the same kitchen, so cross-contamination is possible.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetarian offering is ovo-lacto (includes eggs and dairy) and shares the same kitchen as meat/fish dishes, so cross-contact is possible.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Allergy accommodation is available but requires advance notice when booking.

positives.text: Offers ovo-lacto vegetarian course options and menus featuring seasonal Yamato vegetables.

cultural_comfort.note: As the flagship dining room of a historic international hotel, the staff are used to overseas guests and can handle English, so a foreign student can dine here comfortably — though it is a formal, special-occasion-priced setting rather than a casual everyday spot.

nara_nakamuraya.gf_detail: No documented gluten-free program. The menu centers on Italian cooking with house-made pasta such as tortelloni, so most dishes contain wheat. No dedicated gluten-free preparation or fryer is documented; a strictly gluten-free or celiac diner would need to ask directly and should not assume safe options.
nara_nakamuraya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-oriented restaurant. The cuisine is meat-, fish-, and dairy-forward (game terrines, acqua pazza fish, butter-sauce pasta, cheese). No vegan menu is documented; a vegan diner would need to call ahead, and options would likely be very limited.
nara_nakamuraya.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–15:30 (L.O. 13:30), Dinner 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 20:00); wine bar/café service throughout. Irregular days off.
nara_nakamuraya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner-chef Kohei Nakamura trained at a Tokyo restaurant before apprenticing in Italy, where he learned cooking across both mountainous central regions and the coastal north. He is also a certified sommelier and returns to Italy each year to research current flavors and trends so

chef_bio.background: The owner-chef, Nakamura, trained at a Tokyo restaurant before apprenticing in Italy, where he learned cooking across both mountainous central regions and the coastal north. He is also a certified sommelier and returns to Italy each year to research current flavors and trends so he can serve them in Nara.
chef_bio.philosophy: To bring the true taste of Italy to Nara's old town - 'to provide the taste of the authentic place as much as possible.' The venue is split into a casual front wine bar and cafe and a more formal dining room in back, letting guests choose their experience.
chef_bio.specialty: Authentic regional Italian cooking using carefully chosen seasonal ingredients: house-made tortelloni in sage-butter sauce, fresh fish acqua pazza, and winter game such as a wild-boar and foie gras terrine made with meat from Tsuge Village near the Nara-Mie border, served with a red-wine (Barolo) gelée. Around 200 Italian wines, including Piedmont Barolo and Tuscan Brunello, served in glassware matched to each pour.

anecdotes.text: The front bar functions as a wine bar and cafe with an Italian barista, Andrea Picchioni, manning the espresso counter, while the back room serves refined course meals on Richard Ginori porcelain with Riedel glassware and Baccarat tumblers.
For winter dishes the chef sources game meat from Tsuge Village near the Nara-Mie prefectural border, reflecting a blend of authentic Italian technique and local Nara ingredients.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: JR-Central's Nara feature and the restaurant's own site confirm an Italy-trained, sommelier-qualified owner-chef (surname Nakamura) who visits Italy yearly, a front winebar&cafe plus back restaurant, ~200 Italian wines (Barolo/Brunello), Andrea Picchioni as barista, Richard Ginori tableware with Riedel/Baccarat glassware, sage-butter tortelloni, acqua pazza, and Tsuge-Village game terrine with Barolo gelée. Chef's given name not published; 'Limoges' in the prior draft was unsupported.

cultural_comfort.note: A warm but refined Italian spot where a few words of Japanese help; an Italian barista works the front bar, so basic communication is manageable, but the dinner courses run higher in price than a casual student meal.

nara_pe_loncho_2.gf_detail: This is a teppan hamburger and steak house. Hamburger patties contain binders and the dishes are served with onion/red-wine sauces; no gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no documented celiac protocols. Not suitable for strict gluten-free or celiac diners.
nara_pe_loncho_2.vegan_detail: A meat-focused restaurant whose entire concept is coarse-ground beef/pork hamburger steak and rare beef steak. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
nara_pe_loncho_2.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–14:30 (L.O. 14:00) daily except Tuesday; Dinner 18:00–21:30 (L.O. 20:30) Wed–Sun & holidays. Monday is lunch only. Tuesday closed. Some irregular/event closures and year-end/New Year holidays.

chef_bio.background: PE LONCHO opened in December 2019 in the Takabatake area at the eastern end of Naramachi-dori, closer to Nara Park. It is a small, independent teppan (iron-griddle) restaurant built around two signature plates: a thick coarse-ground hamburger steak and a thick-cut, rare beef steak, each served sizzling on a hot iron plate.
chef_bio.specialty: Coarse-ground teppan hamburger steak and rare beef steak (around 250g portions). The hamburger blends Yamato beef, chuck roll and Kazaguruma pork in a secret ratio, finished with a sauce built on plenty of onions and red wine.

anecdotes.text: The signature hamburger recipe is said to have been handed down from a well-known Italian-cuisine chef in the Sangenjaya area of Tokyo.
The kitchen serves a limited number of meals per day (around 50), reflecting a small, hands-on operation.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: naralunch.com confirms a December 2019 opening in Takabatake near Naramachi-dori and ~250g portions; narakko.jp confirms the coarse-ground hamburger of Yamato beef, chuck roll and Kazaguruma pork in a秘伝 secret blend with an onion-and-red-wine sauce, and roughly 50 servings a day (6 tables, 9 counter seats).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Hamburger steak is a core dish and typically contains wheat-based binders; sauces are onion/red-wine based with no stated gluten-free preparation.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Entirely a beef/pork teppan concept (hamburger and steak); no vegan or vegetarian dishes are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local teppan spot where ordering is smoother in Japanese, and because mains must be reserved in advance to secure stock, a foreign student should phone or message ahead (ideally with a Japanese-speaking friend).

nara_toi_inshokuten_2.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination and no celiac protocol is documented. The meals plate centers on rice (jasmine/Nara rice) and many spice-based vegetable sides, which can lean naturally wheat-free, but fried items such as pakoda fritters and papad (lentil wafers) may contain or be cross-contacted by wheat, and the daily curries are made in a shared kitchen with no dedicated equipment noted. A celiac traveler must ask in person about each component; nothing specific is published.
nara_toi_inshokuten_2.vegan_detail: The fixed meals format pairs a choice of curries (which on most days include meat/fish options such as fish, mutton, chicken or pork curries) with a large spread of roughly eight vegetable sides — e.g. coconut-stir-fried carrots, mustard-simmered yam and taro, leafy-green and red-radish kachumbar salad, dal, achar pickles and chutneys. A vegetable curry is usually available so a largely plant-based meals plate can be assembled, but the kitchen has not published whether dals/sides use ghee, dairy or any fish/animal stock, and it is not a dedicated vegetarian/vegan kitchen. Vegans should confirm dairy (ghee/yogurt) and stock in person.
nara_toi_inshokuten_2.hours_raw: Wed, Thu 11:30–14:30 / Fri, Sat 11:30–14:30, 17:30–20:30 / closed Mon, Tue, Sun
nara_toi_inshokuten_2.notes: The owner-chef honed his craft at established Nara Indian and curry kitchens — including time as chef at an Indian cafe-restaurant in Tomigaoka and a monthly pop-up at a spot in Ayameike — and made a multi-week journey through India to deepen his feel for regional cooking before

chef_bio.background: The owner-chef honed his craft at established Nara Indian and curry kitchens — including time as chef at an Indian cafe-restaurant in Tomigaoka and a monthly pop-up at a spot in Ayameike — and made a multi-week journey through India to deepen his feel for regional cooking before opening his own place in February 2021 in the Hanashiba-cho area just north of Kintetsu Nara Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Indian food adapted to Nara's climate and local produce, plated like a jewel box but meant to be mixed and eaten by hand — the chef describes treating the plate as a palette and adjusting the flavors with your fingers as you go.
chef_bio.specialty: A daily-changing 'meals' (ミールス) plate: a choice of one to four curries that rotate each day — spanning South Indian chicken, Kerala-style seafood, vindaloo and vegetable curries — served around rice with about eight sides such as coconut-stir-fried carrots, mustard-simmered yam and taro, dal, kachumbar salad, achar pickles, chutneys, pakoda fritters and crisp lentil papad.

anecdotes.text: The chef frames authentic Indian dining as hands-on: '皿をパレットに見立て、指で調理しながら食べるのがインド流' — treat the plate as a palette and season as you eat with your fingers.
Local curry writers greeted the 2021 opening as 'a supernova born in Nara,' noting the chef's pedigree at earlier Nara kitchens (Tomigaoka's 'phool' and the Ayameike popup 'praana').

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: serai.jp confirms the owner-chef ('Tamu') made a three-week India trip, opened toi印食店 in Feb 2021 in Hanashiba-cho near Kintetsu Nara, and serves a 1–4 curry meals plate with ~8 sides plus the 皿をパレットに見立て hand-eating quote; kareota.com confirms his prior roles at Tomigaoka's 'phool' and the Ayameike monthly popup 'praana' and the '奈良の地に超新星が誕生' welcome.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The plate includes fried pakoda fritters and crisp lentil papad/appalam, which commonly involve wheat or shared frying oil; no gluten-free protocol is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Curries on most days include fish, mutton, chicken or pork options served from the same daily lineup as the vegetable curry; sides' use of ghee/dairy or any stock is not published.

positives.text: The fixed meals format includes a wide range of vegetable sides (coconut carrots, mustard yam and taro, dal, kachumbar salad, pickles, chutneys) so a largely plant-based plate can usually be assembled.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, popular counter shop with no reservations — write your name in the entry ledger and wait; a few words of Japanese and patience go a long way, and the hand-eating Indian style is welcomed.

nara_the_burger_stand_maveric_2.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The core product is a burger on a natural-yeast wheat bun (baked in a stone oven), and there is no documented gluten-free bun or accommodation. The signature Luther Burger uses a wheat donut in place of the bun. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_the_burger_stand_maveric_2.vegan_detail: A grass-fed beef burger shop; the menu is built around beef patties, bacon, cheese and egg. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
nara_the_burger_stand_maveric_2.hours_raw: 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:30) / 17:00-20:00 (L.O. 19:30); may close early when sold out

chef_bio.origin: Naramachi (Fukuchiin-cho), then relocated to Kitabukuro-cho, Nara City
chef_bio.background: A small independent burger stand that began near Fukuchiin Temple in the southern part of Naramachi and in early 2025 relocated to a spot on the north side of Nara Women's University, a short walk from the heart of central Nara. The interior leans full Americana: counter seats and a couple of tables, oldies playing, and American-themed décor on the walls.
chef_bio.philosophy: A commitment to lean, firm grass-fed beef and from-scratch buns, served in an unpretentious, all-American counter setting.
chef_bio.specialty: Craft hamburgers built on patties made exclusively from grass-fed beef, served on natural-yeast buns slow-baked in a stone oven until the surface turns crisp. Standouts include the Cheese Burger, the Bacon Egg Cheese Burger, and the playful Luther Burger, which swaps the bun for a house-made glazed donut layered with bacon and cheese for a sweet-and-savory bite. Burgers come in a classic style with lettuce and tomato or a bread-and-meat-forward American style, and arrive with a side salad.

anecdotes.text: The shop's mascot, Maverick-kun, is said to have a hobby of collecting insects.
The Luther Burger sandwiches the patty between a self-made sugar-glazed donut with bacon and cheese, and reviewers describe its sweet-savory balance as addictive.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet.com and goguynet.jp confirm patties use only グラスフェッドビーフ (grass-fed beef raised on pasture) on 天然酵母 natural-yeast stone-oven buns, the Jan-2025 relocation from Fukuchiin to Kitabukuro-cho north of Nara Women's University, the Luther Burger's house glazed-donut 'bun', classic vs American styles with a side salad, and mascot Maverick-kun's insect-collecting hobby.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The Teriyaki Burger uses a Japanese soy-based sauce, which typically contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: An easygoing American-style burger stand with an English menu, so a foreign student can order comfortably; just bring cash since cards are not accepted.

nara_cafe_tanne_2.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free establishment. Some menu items lean naturally lower-gluten — buckwheat (soba) pancakes and sprouted brown rice bread — but the café is wheat-using overall (apple pie crust, pastries, pasta), buckwheat pancakes/galettes in Japan are commonly blended with wheat flour, and there is no documented dedicated prep, gluten-free flour sourcing, or cross-contamination control. A celiac diner would need to ask directly about each item; assume shared surfaces and possible wheat in batters.
nara_cafe_tanne_2.vegan_detail: Not a vegan establishment. The kitchen uses animal products throughout — grilled fish and miso soup in the Japanese morning set, ice cream/whipped cream with pancakes, and butter/eggs/dairy in the apple pie and baked sweets. No documented vegan menu or vegan-specific items. A plant-based diner would need to ask what, if anything, can be prepared without animal products; options are likely very limited.
nara_cafe_tanne_2.hours_raw: 8:00–18:00 (morning service 8:00–10:30, lunch from 11:00). Closed Thursdays per the local shopping-street listing; some listings note irregular closures and year-round operation, so confirm before a special trip.

chef_bio.origin: Nara (owner's hometown), with strong ties to Togakushi/Shinshu, Nagano
chef_bio.background: Cafe TANNE is a townhouse café on the Shimomikado shopping street, on the edge of Nara's historic Naramachi district. Its owner spent about 17 years living in Togakushi in Shinshu (Nagano) before returning to their Nara hometown to open the café. The name 'Tanne' means fir tree and carries the owner's affection for Togakushi, described as a second home.
chef_bio.philosophy: Gentle, body-friendly cooking built around seasonal ingredients — many sourced from Nagano — served in a warm, relaxed space aimed at adults who want a calm, nourishing meal or coffee break.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade health-conscious sweets and light meals: a Shinshu apple pie made with Kogyoku (Jonathan) red apples, pancakes made with sprouted brown rice, hot sandwiches on sprouted brown rice bread, and a set-style 'Tanne Lunch.' The sweets menu runs to roughly fifteen items.

anecdotes.text: The owner lived in Togakushi, Shinshu for about 17 years before returning to their Nara hometown to open the café; 'Tanne' means fir tree and expresses their lasting affection for Togakushi as a second home.
Mornings offer a homestyle Japanese set with freshly cooked rice, vegetable miso soup, braised vegetables, grilled fish and pickled plum, alongside Western morning options.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet.com confirms the owner spent ~17 years in Togakushi/Shinshu before returning to their native Nara, that 'Tanne' means fir tree for that region, the Shimomikado-cho location, ~15 desserts, sprouted-brown-rice pancakes with Shinshu (Jonathan/Kogyoku) apples, sprouted-brown-rice-bread hot sandwiches, and Japanese & Western breakfast sets.

positives.text: Some menu items are built on naturally lower-gluten bases such as buckwheat (soba) pancakes and sprouted brown rice bread, which may give flexible (non-celiac) gluten-avoiders something to work with — confirm ingredients with staff.

cultural_comfort.note: A calm, owner-run neighborhood café where a few words of Japanese and a friendly greeting go a long way; English support is not guaranteed, so a translation app helps for asking about ingredients.

nara_cohcu_kohaku.gf_detail: This is a wheat-flour bakery. Bread is the core product (hard-crust loaves, filled breads, bagels, sandwiches), so it is not suitable for gluten-free or celiac diners. No gluten-free items are documented.
nara_cohcu_kohaku.vegan_detail: A traditional bakery whose best-known items contain dairy and egg (the signature cream pan "Kobako" is filled with cold custard cream; other items include curry bread and sandwiches). Plain hard-crust breads may be egg/dairy-free but this is not confirmed; a vegan diner would need to ask about specific loaves. No explicitly vegan items are documented.
nara_cohcu_kohaku.hours_raw: From around 8:00 until sold out (hours/stock announced via SNS etc.). Closed Wed; Tue is an irregular day off.
nara_cohcu_kohaku.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independent neighborhood bakery tucked into a quiet residential block of Horen-cho in northern Nara, near Ichijo High School and a short walk from Shin-Omiya Station. chef_bio.background: A small, independent neighborhood bakery tucked into a quiet residential block of Horen-cho in northern Nara, near Ichijo High School and a short walk from Shin-Omiya Station. The plain, unassuming storefront barely looks like a bakery from outside, but inside it is packed with around thirty kinds of bread laid out invitingly each day.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's own writing stresses making bread 'humbly and earnestly' (謙虚にそして真摯に) out of genuine love for the bread itself.
chef_bio.specialty: Hard-crust, dough-focused breads (including plenty of campagne loaves) alongside generously filled breads. The signature item is a cream pan called 'Kobako' (こはく。のこばこ): the cold custard cream is piped in fresh at the moment of purchase, and it is meant to be eaten right away while the cream is still cold. Other beloved items include a hearty beef curry bread and a sweet-potato cream Danish.

anecdotes.text: The bread is made in limited daily quantity and is famous for selling out fast, sometimes by just after midday, so regulars line up early.
The signature 'Kobako' cream pan (about ¥292) has its cold cream added after you order, and is recommended to be eaten immediately while cold.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ameblo.jp (narakoto10) and web listings confirm this Horen-cho bakery's signature こはく。のこばこ cream pan (~¥292) has its cold cream piped in after ordering and is best eaten at once, that it stocks many campagne/hard breads and often sells out by early afternoon. A reviewer notes the beef curry bread uses 近江牛 Omi beef, so the earlier 'Yamato-beef' attribution was not supported.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A working wheat-flour bakery; flour is used throughout, making cross-contamination unavoidable for gluten-free diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature and popular items contain dairy and egg (custard cream pan, curry bread, sandwiches); shared bakery equipment means egg/dairy contact is likely across products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny neighborhood takeout bakery where ordering is simple point-and-pay; a friendly greeting in Japanese is plenty, though English is unlikely and items sell out by early afternoon.

nara_norr_coffee_roasters_2.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering documented. The food menu centers on wheat-based baked goods such as financiers, pound cake, and Breton galettes, so this is not a safe choice for celiac diners. No allergen handling or gluten-free items are mentioned on any source.
nara_norr_coffee_roasters_2.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. As a coffee shop the black filter coffees and coffee tonic soda are plant-based, but milk-based drinks (cafe latte) and the baked sweets (financier, pound cake, galette) typically contain dairy and eggs. A vegan visitor could likely have a black coffee but should ask about everything else; no plant-milk options are confirmed.
nara_norr_coffee_roasters_2.hours_raw: Sundays only, approx. 13:00-18:00 (last order around 16:45). The owner works on weekdays, so the shop opens only on Sundays; an "öppet" (Swedish for "open") sign is displayed when trading. Note: an older listing shows weekday 11:00-16:30 and Sunday 11:00-17:00 hours, which appears to be outdated. Confirm via the shop's social media before visiting.
nara_norr_coffee_roasters_2.notes: [Mom & Pop] NORR Coffee Roasters is a small self-roasting specialty coffee shop tucked into the quiet Kitamachi residential area in northern central Nara, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner keeps a weekday job and opens the shop only on Sundays, hanging out an 'öppet' sign —

chef_bio.background: NORR Coffee Roasters is a small self-roasting specialty coffee shop tucked into the quiet Kitamachi residential area in northern central Nara, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner keeps a weekday job and opens the shop only on Sundays, hanging out an 'öppet' sign — Swedish for 'open' — when trading. The name NORR means 'north' in Swedish, a nod to the shop's location in the northern Kitamachi district and its Nordic-inflected sensibility.
chef_bio.philosophy: Uses 100% specialty-grade beans, roasting to emphasize each coffee's natural sweetness, and runs the space as both a roastery cafe and a rotating art gallery for a slow, leisurely atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted single-origin specialty coffees (four varieties available hot or iced, from origins such as Brazil, Honduras, Guatemala, Indonesia, El Salvador, Tanzania, Rwanda and more) plus a house 'NORR Blend' roasted to bring out natural sweetness. Also coffee tonic soda and frozen coffee, alongside baked sweets such as Breton galettes.

anecdotes.text: The space doubles as a gallery, with rotating artwork, three single seats by the entrance, a mezzanine with tables upstairs, and a semi-underground terrace facing a courtyard.
Limited-edition coffee packages are released to celebrate local Nara events such as the Todaiji water ceremony and the Wakakusayama grass-burning festival.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet.com confirms the Sundays-only roastery in Kitamachi (owner keeps a weekday job), the öppet sign, NORR='north' in Swedish, four hot/iced specialty coffees, coffee tonic and frozen coffee, the gallery function with three counter seats, an upstairs mezzanine and a semi-underground courtyard terrace, and that baked items (Breton galettes) come from toko cafe. The shop's own store lists festival-themed limited coffee packages.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, relaxed Nordic-themed coffee shop where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you by, though staff may not speak much English and the Sunday-only hours mean you should check before making the trip.

nara_jizake_bar_nara_sake_bar.gf_detail: No gluten-free program. Sake itself is rice-based and naturally wheat-free, so the core tasting flights are fine for someone avoiding wheat. However the food snacks are a different matter: cured/smoked items and seasonings commonly involve soy sauce (which contains wheat) and there is no allergen labeling or celiac handling here. Treat it as a drinking spot where the sake is the safe item and any food should be questioned individually. Not a celiac-safe kitchen.
nara_jizake_bar_nara_sake_bar.vegan_detail: Primarily a sake bar; the food leans heavily on game meat (house-made venison jerky, wild boar smoked ham) and other animal products (smoked eggs, sweetfish). A few plant-based snacks exist — smoked tofu and pickled vegetables (漬物) — but these are likely seasoned with non-vegan dashi or soy-based marinades and are not advertised as vegan. The sake flights are the main vegan-friendly draw. Suitable for a vegan only as a place to drink with a token plant snack, not for a meal.
nara_jizake_bar_nara_sake_bar.hours_raw: 11:00–16:00 (Tuesdays 11:00–15:00). Hours have varied over time (earlier listings showed 10:00–18:00 / 11:00–17:00); confirm before visiting.

chef_bio.background: This standing sake bar sits on the ground floor of Nara Nagomi-kan, a souvenir hall facing the historic Nara Hotel in the Takabatake district. The hall once thrived on bus tours and school excursions, but when the pandemic erased that crowd in 2020, the director, Yamaji Junichi, shrank the gift-shop floor and reinvented the space as a place to drink. The bar opened on April 29, 2021, drawing on know-how from a sister project, a sake bar in Tohoku that had been running since 2013 as part of the region's earthquake-recovery efforts.
chef_bio.philosophy: The bar deliberately serves two crowds at once: an everyday neighborhood stop for locals, and a way for travelers to taste Nara's breweries and make a memory of the trip.
chef_bio.specialty: Nara and Tohoku local sake tasting flights

anecdotes.text: The bar is a COVID-era reinvention: with tour buses and school trips gone, Nagomi-kan downsized its souvenir section and opened a standing sake bar in its place in spring 2021.
The chef hunts the game himself, turning venison and wild boar into house-made jerky and smoked ham served as sake pairings.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara.keizai.biz (Apr 2021) confirms the April 29 2021 opening, hall director Yamaji Junichi (山地淳一) downsizing the souvenir floor after COVID, the Tohoku sister bar running since 2013, and chef-hunter Morisugi Kenichi (森杉健一), a six-year hunter who butchers his own game. nara-gourmet confirms the venison jerky / wild-boar smoked ham pairings and the 3-item tasting flights.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Snacks include cured, smoked, and pickled items typical of a sake bar, which commonly use soy-sauce-based seasonings (soy sauce normally contains wheat); no gluten-free claims are made.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Food program centers on house-made venison and wild boar, so plant snacks like smoked tofu and pickles are prepared in a meat-handling environment.

positives.text: Sake is rice-based and naturally free of wheat and animal products, so the tasting flights are inherently safe for both wheat-avoidant and vegan drinkers.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual standing sake bar inside a tourist-friendly souvenir hall near Nara Hotel where tasting sets are priced for walk-ins, so a foreign student can comfortably point at a flight and enjoy it with a few words of Japanese.

nara_shichifuku_shokudo_kissa.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The monthly lunch sets are built around dishes such as tempura, chilled wheat noodles, fu (wheat gluten / seitan) and seasonal Japanese home cooking, and the menu uses standard Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, etc.) that contain wheat. There is no indication of a dedicated fryer or gluten-free preparation. Celiac travelers should not consider this safe.
nara_shichifuku_shokudo_kissa.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian place. The monthly teishoku centers on meat and fish — e.g. pork Yanagawa-style hotpot, shrimp/mushroom chirashi sushi, mozuku vinegar — and most dishes use fish dashi. Vegetable side dishes (namul, seasonal Yamato/local produce) and the parfaits/coffee exist but are not prepared as guaranteed vegan, and dashi/honey/dairy are likely present. A vegan traveler would have very limited safe options and should ask directly.

chef_bio.origin: Saitama Prefecture (Koshigaya); moved to Nara in 2007 to study Buddhist art at Nara University
chef_bio.background: Sakai grew up in Koshigaya, Saitama, with little exposure to temples until a middle-school trip to Kyoto, where the fierce, dynamic Buddhist statues at Toji (the Five Great Wisdom Kings) lit a lifelong fascination. He chose Nara University specifically for its cultural-heritage program and its closeness to countless Buddhist statues, then decided to make Nara his permanent home. He runs the guesthouse 古白 (Kohaku, started 2015), which offers Buddhist-statue talks and sukiyaki dinners, added a cafe and renamed it 古白 in 2018, and opened 七福食堂 in 2020 to reach a wider audience.
chef_bio.philosophy: Sakai talks about wanting to 'light the spark' that draws people into Nara's charm, treating a lodging, a cafe or a plate of food as an inviting entry point. He even compares a beautiful parfait to a Buddhist statue: both are tangible, attractive forms that can lead someone toward a deeper appreciation of Nara's culture.
chef_bio.specialty: A monthly-rotating teishoku (set lunch) of seasonal Japanese home cooking — past menus have featured sukiyaki-style pork with a soft-set egg, shrimp-shiitake-and-lotus-root chirashi sushi, tempura, miso-glazed fresh fu (nama-fu dengaku), somen, mozuku vinegar and colorful namul (some months turn Korean, with samgyetang) — alongside a single seasonal parfait (such as caramel-nut and baked-apple, or peach-and-chamomile) and house-roasted drip coffee.

anecdotes.text: The shop occupies a renovated former printing workshop, with a high ceiling, a glass frontage, antique tansu chests and old dishware that give the small room a calm, lived-in feel.
Sakai compares an enticing parfait to a Buddhist statue — a visible 'entry point' meant to spark curiosity in people (even high-schoolers) who might otherwise never engage with Nara's heritage.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-tabikura's interview confirms Sakai Yuki's Koshigaya/Saitama roots, the Toji Five Wisdom Kings spark, his single application to Nara University's cultural-properties program, the 2015 guesthouse, 2018 cafe/rename to Kohaku, 2020 Shichifuku Shokudo, and the parfait-as-Buddhist-statue idea. naralunch and co-trip confirm the renovated printing-workshop room and the monthly single-set format (chirashi with shrimp/shiitake/lotus root, tempura, nama-fu dengaku, mozuku vinegar, namul; a summer peach-chamomile parfait); nara-gourmet confirms the sukiyaki-style pork set and a caramel-nut/baked-apple parfait. The earlier 'Yanagawa-style pork' and 'rum-raisin/chestnut Mont Blanc' parfaits were not in any source and were corrected/removed.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Lunch sets regularly include wheat-based items (tempura, chilled wheat noodles, miso-glazed fu/seitan), so wheat is handled throughout the small kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes use standard Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, miso glaze) which contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is meat- and fish-centered (pork hotpot, shrimp chirashi, mozuku) and most dishes use fish dashi, so vegan separation is not maintained.

positives.text: Cooking emphasizes seasonal local and Yamato/Nara-area vegetables (e.g. produce from a farm in Ikoma), so plant-forward side dishes are part of the meal even though they are not certified vegan.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run shokudo-cafe in old Naramachi where the menu changes monthly and is mostly posted in Japanese on Instagram, so a few words of Japanese (or pointing and a friendly konnichiwa) will go a long way.

chef_bio.background: Shika san chocolat opened in late 2023 as a one-product specialty stand inside the Yume CUBE, the entrepreneur-support corner of Nara's historic Mochiidono Center-gai shopping arcade. Its owner runs it as a second venture alongside Milleturu, a women's tailoring atelier based in nearby Yamato-Koriyama, and spent more than a decade perfecting a single idea: a gateau au chocolat unlike any other.
chef_bio.philosophy: The maker set out to create 'a new standard no one has tasted before,' framing the chocolate-to-sansho transition as a journey ending in Nara, the terminus of the Silk Road. The flourless approach is central to the recipe rather than an afterthought.
chef_bio.specialty: A sansho (Japanese mountain pepper) gateau au chocolat — a rich-but-clean-finishing, fluffy-yet-moist chocolate cake in which the chocolate slowly gives way to bright Japanese-pepper notes, using stone-ground 'budo-sansho' from the Kii Peninsula. It is made entirely without wheat flour, rice flour or baking powder. Sold by the cut, half, and whole cake; a plain version without sansho is also offered for those who prefer it.

anecdotes.text: The signature sansho gateau au chocolat was developed over roughly 15 years of trial and error, using stone-ground Japanese pepper, before the shop opened in 2023.
The owner also runs a women's tailoring business, Milleturu, in Yamato-Koriyama, and treats the chocolate shop as a parallel creative project.
Staff are known for offering free taste samples and explaining the cake to passers-by at the stall.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms the 15-year development, the 'new standard no one has tasted' concept, the Silk-Road-to-Nara framing, stone-ground budo-sansho from the Kii Peninsula, and no wheat/rice flour or baking powder. goguynet confirms the 2023 opening in Yume CUBE, the Milleturu tailoring atelier in Yamato-Koriyama, slice/half/whole pricing and free samples. mochiidono confirms a plain 'sansho-nuki' (no-pepper) version is also offered. No owner name is published anywhere.

positives.text: The signature gateau au chocolat is made with no wheat flour and no rice flour, so the core product is naturally gluten-free by recipe.

nara_kaiseki_ryori_en_yen_2.vegan_detail: The kitchen is vegetable-centric and the official site explicitly advertises vegetarian guidance, so plant-forward meals are possible with advance reservation, but the default kaiseki uses fish dashi and includes fish/egg dishes; vegans must call ahead to confirm.

chef_bio.background: A small, independent kaiseki house in Nara's Naramachi district run by its proprietor for more than 30 years (since around 1987), on the second floor of a building along the Shimo-mikado arcade a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Letting Nara's seasonal vegetables and local Yamato specialties shine; menus rotate with the seasons. The owner added a weekend breakfast in response to requests from nearby guesthouse guests wanting an early seasonal Nara meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable-forward seasonal kaiseki at an approachable price. Two signature dishes are sake-lees tempura and miso-marinated tofu. It is also one of the few places in Nara still serving the local specialty chagayu (tea-steeped rice porridge), offered as a set and as a swap for plain rice at breakfast.

anecdotes.text: A diner praised the smooth feel of the tea porridge and the careful knife work in the thoughtfully cut vegetables.
The breakfast (around 650 yen, 8:00-10:00) was introduced in response to an increase in nearby guesthouses whose guests wanted an early seasonal Nara meal.
Described as a calm, hidden upstairs space with no background music and traditional decor including samurai-armor displays and fresh flowers, with windows over Naramachi.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official yen-kaiseki.com confirms the Shimo-mikado 2F address, 30+ years (a 33rd anniversary noted in 2020) and the chagayu set. naramati-nararaku confirms the ~650-yen 8-10am breakfast, the guesthouse-request origin, the chagayu-or-rice choice, careful vegetable knife work, the no-BGM room and samurai-armor/flower decor. naralunch corroborates the signatures (sake-lees tempura, miso-marinated tofu) and the quiet upstairs feel. No proprietor name is published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature dish is sake-lees tempura (wheat batter) and summer menus include somen (wheat noodles); cooking relies on soy-based seasonings and fish/kombu dashi. No gluten-free protocol is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Standard kaiseki includes fish dishes (salted grilled mackerel) and dashi/egg; the kitchen is not vegan by default, so vegans must request plant-only preparation in advance.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The official site advertises guidance for vegetarian guests; reservations by phone with menu choice stated in advance are recommended, allowing accommodation to be discussed ahead.

positives.text: Vegetable-centric seasonal cooking and explicit willingness to provide vegetarian guidance, with advance phone reservation, make plant-forward meals feasible.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, traditional family-run kaiseki spot where the proprietor cooks and serves personally; phone ahead in basic Japanese to reserve and state your menu choice, and be comfortable in a calm, mostly Japanese-speaking setting.

chef_bio.background: Gentry first opened in April 1984 as an old-school jazz bar in central Nara, spinning jazz on vinyl and hosting occasional live performances. Over four decades it became beloved less for its records than for an unlikely signature: an elaborate flambeed shaved ice. After closing its long-time home in the Shimomikado shopping street in April 2024 to the sadness of many regulars, it returned in late October 2025 a few steps from Kintetsu Nara Station, now billed as Kakigori & Whisky Gentry, still built around its Swan ice shaver and jazz-bar mood.
chef_bio.specialty: The house specialty is yaki-gori, baked shaved ice: layers of azuki beans, lemon jelly and condensed milk under a matcha meringue that the owner blowtorches to a caramelized crust, then douses with flambeed Cointreau so the mountain of ice briefly catches fire, a nod to Nara's Wakakusa-yama grass-burning festival. Seasonal creations rotate through flavors such as pistachio and white chocolate, pumpkin, strawberry, and custard brulee. By night it pours whisky, wine and cocktails.

anecdotes.text: The signature baked shaved ice is set alight tableside with flambeed orange liqueur, an edible homage to the Wakakusa-yama mountain-burning that lights up the Nara skyline each winter.

Founded in April 1984, the shop closed its original location in April 2024 and pre-opened at its new spot near the station on 23 October 2025; the owner is remembered by visitors for a bright, courteous manner.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet confirms the jazz-bar heritage, the flambeed matcha-meringue yaki-gori (azuki, lemon jelly, condensed milk) with Cointreau and the Wakakusa-yama homage, plus night whisky/wine/cocktails and a pistachio version. note.com confirms the April 1984 founding, April 2024 closure, the Swan-brand ice shaver and the owner's bright manner. Tabelog (29015211) confirms the new address ~146m from Kintetsu Nara Station with a 23 October 2025 pre-open.

cultural_comfort.note: A warm, owner-run jazz bar where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the photo menu will get you the famous flambéed shaved ice; the master is known for being friendly and polite, so a beginner can manage comfortably.

chef_bio.chef_name: 廣岡夏主 (Hirooka Natsushi, who goes by the nickname "Nassh")
chef_bio.background: The owner ran a creative izakaya near JR Nara Station for roughly six years before relocating in January 2024 to a quietly renovated machiya (traditional townhouse) in the Naramachi district, near the Imanishi Seibei brewery (maker of Harushika sake). He runs the entire nine-seat counter single-handedly.
chef_bio.philosophy: He builds dishes on a French, Italian and Spanish base and fuses them with Japanese seasonings — dashi, soy sauce and miso — describing his aim as expanding 'new possibilities in food,' an idea he links to the cultural mixing of the Silk Road that historically reached Nara.
chef_bio.specialty: Cold-smoking (冷燻): the homemade smoked assortment — which can include prosciutto, quail egg, oyster and scallop — is the most-ordered dish. Other signatures pair Nara produce with European technique, such as cold peach pasta with Yamato beef prosciutto, young-corn fritters with white-miso aioli, and a 'wa-hijo' (Japanese-style ajillo) of firefly squid and rape blossoms.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen makes a point of using Nara-region ingredients — Yamato pork, Yamato chicken and Yamato beef — alongside local sake and hand-pulled Miwa somen noodles.
An earlier black-rice curry of the owner's took second place in a 2010 curry competition (National Curry Championship).
The current space is a renovated townhouse with a single nine-seat wooden-slab counter, sitting near the Imanishi Seibei (Harushika) brewery and the acclaimed hand-pulled soba restaurant Kurogane.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The cooking is explicitly built on dashi, soy sauce and miso as its Japanese seasoning base, all of which typically contain or accompany wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat counter run solo by the owner in a renovated townhouse; basic Japanese helps a great deal as English service should not be assumed, and the intimate setting rewards diners comfortable with a quiet, local atmosphere.

chef_bio.background: SomechoA (サムチョア) is a small Korean-style day cafe and night bar tucked along Sanjo-dori a couple of minutes from JR Nara Station, between the JR and Kintetsu Nara stations. It is run by three siblings, and the name itself reflects that: in Korean 'Sam' means 'three' and 'choA' means 'like/love,' so the place is built around the trio and the things they love.
chef_bio.philosophy: A relaxed hideaway that doubles as a lunch and night cafe and an evening drinking spot, filling the room with the siblings' favorite Korean food, sweets, and drinks.
chef_bio.specialty: Korean fried chicken — the most popular item — with a crispy batter and house-made sauce, a creamy tomato (rose) tteokbokki, seafood pancakes (chijimi), and night-cafe desserts including handmade gateau chocolate and New York cheesecake sold from the entrance showcase. A signature playful item is the Nara-themed 'deer pudding,' a local twist on Korea's animal-shaped puddings.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name comes from Korean: 'Sam' (three) plus 'choA' (like/love), referring to the three siblings who run it and pack it with their favorite things.
They make a Nara-exclusive deer-shaped pudding, a regional riff on the trendy animal-shaped Korean puddings.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hotpepper (official listing) states the name サムチョア is a cafe 'packed with the likes of the three siblings who run it,' with 'Sam' = Korean for three and 'choA' = like/love, and places it on Sanjo-dori 2 min from JR Nara Station. owst confirms Korean fried chicken as the No.1 item, the rose (tomato-cream) tteokbokki, seafood chijimi, and the Nara-exclusive deer pudding. The original somechoa-nara.com source is offline and was replaced.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core menu items use wheat: yangnyeom fried chicken has a fried wheat batter, and seafood pancakes (pajeon) and tteokbokki are wheat-based, sharing a kitchen with no documented separation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Korean sauces such as the house yangnyeom sauce typically rely on wheat-containing soy sauce and gochujang; no gluten-free sauces are indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward (Korean fried chicken, seafood pancakes) and desserts use dairy/eggs, so vegan cross-contact is likely and unmanaged.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, youthful Korean cafe-bar run by young owners where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will carry you through, though detailed allergy questions may be hard without some Japanese.

nara_savas_cafe_2.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The menu centers on wheat-based dishes: gratin served over pasta or inside a baguette, sandwiches, and chiffon cakes (made with wheat flour). No gluten-free options or accommodations are documented, and this is not a celiac-safe destination.
nara_savas_cafe_2.vegan_detail: Not a vegan destination. Signature items use dairy and animal products: gratin includes cheese, cream/bechamel, salmon, chicken or hamburger, while chiffon cakes use eggs and dairy. A plant-based eater would have very limited options and should ask in advance; no vegan menu is documented.
nara_savas_cafe_2.hours_raw: 10:00-19:00; closed Wednesdays (open if Wednesday is a public holiday)

chef_bio.background: SAVAS CAFE sits in a crisp white one-house building along Yasuragi-no-michi, right beside Isagawa Shrine and just a few minutes' walk from the bustle of Kintetsu Nara Station. The cafe spreads over two floors: a takeout and retail counter on the ground floor, and an airy upstairs dining room with high ceilings, white walls, cheerful red accents on the window frames and furniture, and big windows looking out over the street. A ceiling fan keeps the room comfortable even in summer.
chef_bio.philosophy: The place is run with a clear emphasis on comfort and relaxation — staff will even suggest the best seat for the temperature that day, a small touch that captures the cafe's attentive, unhurried spirit.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen is built around two homemade specialties: gratin and chiffon cake. The gratin comes either baked in an ovenproof dish over macaroni or tucked inside a baguette, with fillings that rotate through combinations like salmon and corn, spinach and chicken, or hamburger and broccoli, typically served as a set with salad and a drink. The chiffon cakes are the other star — light, finely textured and only gently sweet, offered in around five rotating varieties such as matcha, blueberry, cocoa-banana and a summer salt-roasted version. A houjicha (roasted-tea) jelly parfait and fruit-and-custard parfaits round out the dessert menu.

anecdotes.text: Staff proactively recommend the most comfortable seat depending on the temperature, reflecting the cafe's relaxed, guest-first attitude.
The chiffon cakes come in around five rotating varieties, including seasonal flavors such as matcha, blueberry, cocoa-banana and a summer salt-roasted version.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: naramati-nararaku confirms the location beside Isagawa Shrine near Kintetsu Nara Station, the two-floor layout, the staff seat-by-temperature service, the three gratin fillings (salmon-corn, spinach-chicken, hamburger-broccoli with macaroni), and the ~550-yen houjicha jelly parfait. nara-gourmet confirms the gratin (dish or baguette) and 'about five varieties including seasonal' chiffon cakes. The earlier 'well over a hundred recipes' claim was contradicted (five varieties) and corrected; 'Yamato tea' was unverified and softened to houjicha.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed neighborhood cafe where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will carry you through; bring cash and don't expect English support.

nara_nara_izumi_yusai.gf_detail: This is a sake tasting bar, not a kitchen. Sake (junmai/ginjo) is brewed from rice, water and koji and is generally gluten-free, so the core offering of by-the-glass tastings is broadly suitable. However, this is not a celiac-focused venue and there is no published allergen handling. Accompanying small plates include items such as hishio (a koji-based fermented seasoning), aged sake-lees cream cheese and Nara pickles (narazuke) — narazuke and some seasonings are cured in sake lees / may involve soy or barley-derived components, so a sensitive celiac should ask about or avoid the food side and confirm before consuming.
nara_nara_izumi_yusai.vegan_detail: Drinks-focused venue. Most sake is vegan, though sake filtration/processing is not disclosed here. Food is limited to a few snacks: Nara pickles (narazuke) and koji-based hishio are plant-based, but the aged sake-lees cream cheese is dairy. There is no dedicated vegan menu — vegans can taste sake and choose pickle-type snacks but should ask about each item.
nara_nara_izumi_yusai.hours_raw: 11:00–20:00, closed Thursdays (open if Thursday falls on a national holiday); occasional temporary closures announced on the official site.

chef_bio.background: The shop opened in April 2012 in a white-walled traditional townhouse just off the Mochiidono arcade, on a site that had previously been the sake shop Sakagura Sasaya. It occupies a historic merchant quarter near Todai-ji, Kofuku-ji and Gangoji. The proprietor, Shinsuke Yamamoto, is a former researcher and director at Nara's prefectural industrial technology center with a background in fermentation chemistry — expertise he drew on, including work connected to reviving the ancient monk-brewed Bodaisen sake.
chef_bio.philosophy: Celebrates Nara's claim as a birthplace of clear refined sake, giving visitors an approachable, low-commitment way to explore the prefecture's breweries (such as Harushika and Hatsugasumi) and discover a favorite with staff guidance.
chef_bio.specialty: Paid by-the-glass tasting of around 120 regional sake from roughly 30 breweries across Nara Prefecture, poured in small 50cc glasses from about 150 yen, with comparison sets (pure-rice, ginjo, dry) and the option to buy a bottle of anything you like. Snacks lean on Nara's food heritage — hishio (a revived ancient koji seasoning), sake-lees cream cheese and Nara pickles.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a former director of Nara's prefectural industrial technology center with a fermentation-chemistry background, connected to the revival of the ancient monk-brewed Bodaisen sake.
Set in a historic white-walled townhouse off the Mochiidono shopping street, the compact space has a small standing counter and a bright, refined feel.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: small-life confirms the April 2012 opening in a white townhouse off Mochiidono (former Sakagura Sasaya), proprietor Shinsuke Yamamoto (former director of Nara's prefectural industrial technology center, fermentation-chemistry background, Bodaisen revival), ~120 sake from ~30 breweries, 50cc pours from ~150 yen with pure-rice/ginjo/dry comparison sets, sake-lees and Nara-pickle snacks, and a small standing counter. getnews corroborates the refined townhouse setting.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Snacks include hishio (a koji/soy-type fermented seasoning) and Nara pickles cured in sake lees; these can involve wheat/barley or soy-derived components and are not confirmed gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Among the snacks, sake-lees cream cheese is dairy; pickles and hishio are plant-based but no vegan handling is documented.

positives.text: Sake is poured by the glass and bottles are visible in the counter fridge, so you can see exactly what you are served and ask staff about each one.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly counter where staff happily help you pick sake; a few words of Japanese and a willingness to point at the fridge go a long way, and inexpensive 50cc pours make it easy to try without commitment.

nara_chuka_dokoro_seiten.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a Chinese kitchen built around gyoza (wheat wrappers), wheat-based soy sauce, and likely flour-thickened/wok dishes; there is no dedicated gluten-free handling and cross-contact is unavoidable. Not safe for celiac diners.
nara_chuka_dokoro_seiten.vegan_detail: Not a vegan destination. The kitchen centers on Yamato pork, Yamato beef and seafood; signature dishes (gyoza, mapo tofu, vinegar chicken) are meat/fish-based. Even the locally made tofu dishes are cooked in meat- or fish-derived sauces. The gyoza being garlic-free is a flavor choice, not a vegan one. Vegans would need to ask, and options would be very limited at best.
nara_chuka_dokoro_seiten.hours_raw: Lunch 11:00–15:00 (L.O. 14:00/14:10); Dinner 18:00–22:00 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Tuesdays (plus occasional irregular closures).
nara_chuka_dokoro_seiten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, hidden-gem Chinese restaurant tucked down a narrow alley off the Higashimuki shopping street, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run almost single-handedly by its owner-chef, who has relocated the shop at least once over the years.

chef_bio.background: A small, hidden-gem Chinese restaurant tucked down a narrow alley off the Higashimuki shopping street, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run almost single-handedly by its owner-chef, who has relocated the shop at least once over the years.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chef prizes freshness over speed, cutting vegetables to order and avoiding chemical seasonings, building a 'light, gentle and colorful' style of Chinese cooking that leans on Nara-grown ingredients — Yamato pork, Yamato beef, Yamato vegetables and local tofu — to create a distinctly Nara take on Chinese food.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled gyoza filled with Yamato pork and cabbage (softened with added tofu) and made without garlic; and the house mapo tofu, made with locally grown soybean tofu and fragrant Japanese pepper for a savory, brightly numbing heat. Vinegar chicken and a seafood-and-vegetable chanpon are also local favorites.

anecdotes.text: The standard menu is constantly refreshed with new dishes, so regulars find something different to try almost every visit.
It is known among locals as 'the Chinese place where mapo tofu lovers gather,' pairing especially well with aged Nara sake.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet confirms the hidden Higashimuki-alley location, the garlic-free charcoal-grilled Yamato-pork gyoza, the mapo tofu built on local tofu, the Yamato pork/beef/vegetable ingredients, the no-chemical-seasoning/cut-to-order approach, at least one relocation, plus vinegar chicken and chanpon. exploring-nara confirms the 'mapo-tofu lovers gather' tagline and the aged-Nara-sake pairing. Sources disagree on the exact pepper (two Japanese sansho vs four Sichuan varieties) and did not confirm kombu dashi, so those specifics were softened.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Gyoza and other dishes are made with wheat wrappers and almost certainly wheat-based soy sauce in a shared single-cook kitchen; no gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contact should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a Chinese restaurant, dishes are seasoned with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Even tofu and vegetable dishes are cooked alongside and in sauces derived from pork, beef and seafood; vegan separation is not offered.

positives.text: The signature gyoza are made without garlic, which can help diners avoiding garlic specifically (note: this is not related to gluten or vegan needs).

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run Chinese spot down a side alley with no English menu, so a few words of Japanese and pointing at dishes will help; a friendly greeting goes a long way in a place this small.

nara_genkishin_nara.gf_detail: Not gluten-free in any meaningful way. The core menu is wheat ramen and tsukemen — the shop makes its own noodles from domestic wheat flour (and mineral-rich whole-grain wheat flour for the tsukemen), serves gyoza (wheat wrappers), and uses chicken/vegetable/kombu broth typically finished with standard seasonings. No celiac-safe options and no dedicated handling reported.
nara_genkishin_nara.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. This is a chicken-paitan (tori paitan) specialist — broths are simmered from chicken bones, whole chicken and Yamato chicken, and the signature dishes include char siu, soft-boiled egg, shrimp and gyoza. Even the "soymilk" ramen (飛鳥豆乳ラーメン) is built on a chicken paitan base. No vegan menu documented.
nara_genkishin_nara.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00 (L.O. 16:00), 17:30-20:00 (L.O. 20:00). Note: some listings show continuous service to ~21:30-22:00; hours vary by source/season.

chef_bio.origin: Nara (Higashimuki arcade, near Kintetsu Nara Station)
chef_bio.background: A chicken-paitan ramen and tsukemen shop tucked into the Higashimuki covered arcade, a two-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run as part of a small local restaurant group (the Hiten group, which also operates the nearby Chinese kitchen Hiten), and the Nara branch is descended from an earlier ramen shop on the site once known as 'Nara Ramen Aoniyoshi,' rebranded around the end of 2011.
chef_bio.philosophy: An emphasis on a long-simmered, made-from-scratch chicken paitan base and self-made noodles, paired with local Nara rice.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen builds everything on a milky tori paitan broth simmered for hours from chicken bones, whole chicken, vegetables and kombu. The flagship is the chicken-paitan tsukemen, with house-made medium-thick noodles from domestic whole-grain (mineral-rich whole-wheat) flour and Nara-grown rice. Tourist-friendly specials round out the menu, including the lavish Daibutsu (Great Buddha) ramen topped with shrimp tempura, fried mochi, char siu and soft-boiled egg, and the lighter Asuka soy-milk paitan ramen.

anecdotes.text: Each table is fitted with an IH burner so diners can finish the meal by turning the leftover dipping broth, rice and a raw egg into a savory zosui rice porridge or risotto at the table — many regulars say the rice finish is the best part.
The original site once operated as 'Nara Ramen Aoniyoshi' and was known for its Daibutsu (Great Buddha) ramen, which still survives on the current menu after the rebrand to Genkishin.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: small-life confirms the Higashimuki-arcade Nara branch, the Hiten group, the former 'Nara Ramen Aoniyoshi' rebranded ~end 2011, the chicken-paitan broth (bones, whole bird, vegetables, kombu), the table IH-burner rice/zosui finish, and the surviving Daibutsu ramen. nara-gourmet confirms the whole-grain (whole-wheat) house noodles, the Daibutsu ramen toppings (shrimp tempura, fried mochi, char siu, soft egg) and the Asuka soy-milk ramen. The 'Hiten Sange' second shop, 'Yamato local chicken' and 'organic Hinohikari' specifics were unverified and removed/softened.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is central and unavoidable here: house-made wheat ramen/tsukemen noodles, wheat gyoza wrappers, and shared cookware make this unsafe for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are chicken-based (tori paitan from chicken bones, whole chicken and Yamato chicken); toppings include char siu, egg and shrimp. No vegan preparation reported.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual ramen shop right in the tourist-heavy Higashimuki arcade that sees lots of international visitors, so a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you a comfortable, no-pressure meal.

nara_susuruka_susuranka.gf_detail: This is a ramen shop whose entire concept is a wheat-noodle dish. The signature mapo tofu ramen uses standard medium-thick wheat noodles, and the mapo sauce relies on doubanjiang and fermented soybeans (typically wheat-containing) plus a chicken-bone broth. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen handling information. Not suitable for celiacs or anyone needing strict gluten avoidance.
nara_susuruka_susuranka.vegan_detail: The core and signature dish is mapo tofu ramen built on a chicken-bone broth with minced meat and wheat noodles. No vegan or vegetarian version is documented. Tofu is present but the dish is meat- and animal-broth based, so it is not vegan or vegetarian.

chef_bio.chef_name: 西 奈槻 (Nishi Natsuki) & 奥野 亮太郎 (Okuno Ryotaro)
chef_bio.origin: Nara, Japan; founded by Kinki University students
chef_bio.background: Two friends and Kinki University students (Faculty of Agriculture, Department of Aquaculture) started the shop during the 2020 pandemic. Nishi, a former aspiring drummer who felt adrift after giving up that dream, spent the COVID lockdown visiting local Nara business owners to explore his future. On his third visit, the owner of a Naramachi halal ramen shop offered to hand over the space; Nishi immediately called Okuno, a friend known for his cooking and obsession with mapo tofu, who agreed on the spot. They first opened as 'jinniyah / 奈KAMA' in October 2020, then rebranded to 'すするか、すすらんか。' on June 6, 2021.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name means roughly 'Shall we slurp, or shan't we?' — a play on the founder's mantra '結局やるか、やらんかやで' ('In the end it comes down to whether you do it or not'). They see the shop as more than a restaurant: a way to show young people in Japan that they have choices ('日本の若者に選択肢を'), running initiatives like inviting young people to submit recipes and hosting one-day managers to spark conversations about life paths.
chef_bio.specialty: Their flagship is the mapo tofu ramen called '革命物語' (Kakumei Monogatari) — a custom mapo tofu developed specifically for ramen, layering the heat of doubanjiang and fermented soybeans with the richness of a chicken-bone broth over medium-thick smooth noodles. It was described as an unprecedented bowl for Nara Prefecture at the time.

anecdotes.text: The shop took shape through a public consulting session with Nakagawa Atsushi, chairman of Nakagawa Masashichi Shoten, which helped the founders crystallize their mission of giving young people more choices.
The 奈KAMA name combined Nishi's character '奈' with Okuno's nickname 'Kamakiri' before the pair rebranded to the current playful name.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kindaipicks (Kinki University media) gives the full founding story: names, faculty, Oct 2020 奈KAMA opening, June 6 2021 rebrand, 革命物語 950yen dish, and Nakagawa Masashichi Shoten consulting. Official site confirms the mapo-tofu-over-noodles concept.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are the foundation of every bowl and are boiled in shared water; the mapo sauce uses doubanjiang and fermented-soybean pastes that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The mapo tofu base relies on doubanjiang and fermented soybeans, which are conventional wheat-containing fermented seasonings; no wheat-free seasoning is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls are built on a chicken-bone broth with minced meat, so all preparation surfaces and broth contact animal products; no vegan option is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, lively local ramen counter where a basic Japanese greeting and pointing at the signature bowl will get you a long way; the young owners are open-minded and welcoming, but expect Japanese-only ordering and a short wait at busy times.

nara_luu_s_bao_ruuzu_bao.gf_detail: This is a bao (steamed bun) specialist and the buns are made from organic WHEAT flour, so the core product is not gluten-free and the shop is not celiac-safe. Donuts are also wheat-based. No gluten-free menu or wheat-free options are documented. A celiac traveler should not rely on this shop.
nara_luu_s_bao_ruuzu_bao.vegan_detail: Fully vegan / 100% plant-based — the storefront is marked "100% PLANT-BASED" and the shop is described across multiple sources as a 100％ヴィーガン bao specialist. Around 11 varieties of vegan bao (Taiwanese-style burgers, e.g. plant-meat with BBQ sauce and ample vegetables), plus fries sets, vegan donuts, smoothies, matcha drinks, and ice cream. Uses additive-free seasonings and rice oil. No animal ingredients used.
nara_luu_s_bao_ruuzu_bao.hours_raw: Wed–Sun 10:00–16:00 (last food order 15:30); closed Mondays and Tuesdays. One local listing notes 11:00–16:30; the Tabelog listing states 10:00–16:00 (L.O. 15:30).

chef_bio.background: LUU's BAO is a 100% plant-based bao specialist that began in Osaka's Nipponbashi (Nihonbashi/Ebisucho) area and relocated to the historic Naramachi district of Nara on March 15, 2026, settling into a quiet machiya streetscape near Amenokaku Coffee. The storefront announces '100% PLANT-BASED,' and the shop set out to prove that a fully vegan menu can still be hearty and satisfying.
chef_bio.philosophy: Wholesome, body-conscious plant-based eating: the dough is made from organic wheat and steamed in bamboo baskets like a traditional pork bun, fillings are entirely plant-derived, and the kitchen uses additive-free seasonings and rice oil while aiming for filling, satisfying portions without animal products.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan 'bao' — the steamed split bun known as 割包 (guabao), often called a Taiwanese burger. About 11 varieties are offered, including a plant-meat burger with barbecue sauce piled with vegetables, available with a fries set. Sweets include freshly fried vegan donuts, smoothies, matcha drinks, and ice cream.

anecdotes.text: The shop relocated from Osaka's Nipponbashi to Naramachi and opened in Nara on March 15, 2026, choosing a calm machiya building that suits the area's traditional architecture, with an outdoor bench for casual stops.
It is described as a 'hidden celebrity' sweets spot, with freshly fried donuts and ice cream alongside its roughly 11 bao varieties.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: goguynet and nara-gourmet both confirm the Osaka Nipponbashi -> Naramachi (Nakashinyacho 17-2) move, Mar 15 2026 opening, 100% plant-based, ~11 bao, plant-meat BBQ burger with fries set, and vegan donuts/ice cream. No owner name is published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire core product line is wheat-based (steamed bao buns and donuts made from organic wheat flour), so the kitchen is a wheat-heavy environment and is not suitable for celiac diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shop is described as 100% plant-based across all sources, so animal-product cross-contact risk is inherently low; no specific cross-contact procedures are documented.

positives.text: Marked '100% PLANT-BASED' on the storefront and consistently described as a fully vegan bao specialist, so all menu items are plant-based.
Uses additive-free seasonings and rice oil with organic wheat and plant-based fillings.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual, takeout-friendly counter shop with a clearly visible "100% PLANT-BASED" sign and picture-friendly bao, so a foreign student can order comfortably with basic Japanese greetings and pointing, though staff English is not documented.

nara_vegan_ramen_by_playpen_f.gf_detail: This is a ramen shop; the noodles are wheat-based, so the core dishes are not gluten-free and the kitchen is not celiac-safe. One reviewer mentioned a "gluten free" option, but this is unconfirmed by the shop and there is no documented dedicated gluten-free preparation. A celiac traveler should not rely on it; ask directly before ordering.
nara_vegan_ramen_by_playpen_f.vegan_detail: A vegan-ramen-focused shop with around six clearly labeled vegan ramen styles (vegan miso, soy sauce, tomato, vegan "tonkotsu"-style). The vegan miso uses a domestic miso base with vegetables and spices stir-fried in plant oil, topped with broccoli, corn, fried tofu, soy meat, several seaweeds, wood-ear mushroom, green onion and chili threads. Note that the same kitchen also serves genuine pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken paitan ramen, so this is a vegan-friendly shop rather than a 100% vegan kitchen; strict vegans should confirm separate handling.
nara_vegan_ramen_by_playpen_f.hours_raw: 11:00-17:00 (closed Tuesdays). One local listing lists 10:00-17:00 — confirm on arrival.
nara_vegan_ramen_by_playpen_f.notes: Opened on July 29, 2024 in Noborioji-cho, on the second floor of a building between the Shizuka park branch and Mamejika Shokudo, directly across from the Nara National Museum and a step from Nara Park. The space previously housed a Japanese-tea cafe, Chahua.

chef_bio.origin: Second outpost of a vegan ramen concept that started in Osaka's Nishi Ward (Kita-Horie area), where it built a loyal following before expanding to Nara.
chef_bio.background: Opened on July 29, 2024 in Noborioji-cho, on the second floor of a building between the Shizuka park branch and Mamejika Shokudo, directly across from the Nara National Museum and a step from Nara Park. The space previously housed a Japanese-tea cafe, Chahua.
chef_bio.philosophy: Bring approachable, clearly labeled plant-based ramen to one of Japan's most-visited tourist areas so international and vegan diners can eat ramen overlooking the deer of Nara Park.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based ramen built around a vegan miso bowl: a domestic-miso base with vegetables and spices stir-fried in plant oil, generously topped with broccoli, corn, fried tofu, soy meat, several kinds of seaweed, wood-ear mushroom, green onion and chili threads. Other vegan styles include soy-sauce, tomato and a vegan tonkotsu. The shop also cooks non-vegan pork-bone and chicken-paitan bowls.

anecdotes.text: Window counter seats look straight out over Nara Park, so diners can watch the famous deer while eating; reviewers repeatedly note the generous, colorful assortment of toppings and friendly staff.
Sits between the Shizuka park branch and Mamejika Shokudo, opposite the Nara National Museum, in a spot that previously held the Japanese-tea cafe Chahua.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: scramblenara confirms the July 29 2024 opening in Noborioji-cho (former Chahua tea cafe), the expansion from the original Osaka Nishi-ku shop, the neighbouring Shizuka/Mamejika Shokudo location opposite Nara National Museum, and that both vegan and non-vegan (pork-bone, chicken-paitan) bowls are served.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Ramen noodles are wheat-based and the menu is wheat- and broth-heavy; no dedicated gluten-free handling is documented, so the kitchen should be treated as not celiac-safe.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy-sauce and miso ramen styles are offered; standard Japanese soy sauce and miso contain wheat and no wheat-free version is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The same kitchen cooks genuine pork-bone and chicken-paitan ramen alongside the vegan bowls, so shared-equipment cross-contact is possible; strict vegans should confirm handling.

positives.text: Around six clearly labeled vegan ramen options make it easy for plant-based diners to order without ambiguity.
Vegan miso bowl is built on a domestic miso base with vegetables stir-fried in plant oil and plant-based toppings (fried tofu, soy meat, seaweed, vegetables).

cultural_comfort.note: Very foreigner-friendly with clearly labeled vegan options and a heavily international clientele, so a foreign student can order comfortably with little Japanese.

nara_mikasa_kanko_kaikan.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation is documented. The menu is built on wheat-heavy dishes (tonkatsu, katsu curry with roux, hamburg, udon) and Japanese set meals that rely on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi. There is no indication of gluten-free preparation, separate fryers, or allergy handling, so this is not suitable for celiacs.
nara_mikasa_kanko_kaikan.vegan_detail: The official menu lists a Buddhist-vegetarian (精進料理 / shōjin) set at roughly 1,650–2,350 yen, which is plant-forward by tradition, but its vegan status is not confirmed — shōjin sets in Japan commonly include items prepared with non-vegan dashi or other animal-derived seasonings, and no allergen/vegan information is published. A traveler must confirm directly. The rest of the menu (tonkatsu, hamburg, curry, kamameshi, teppanyaki) is omnivore. The black-soybean soy-milk vegan soft serve mentioned in some listings could not be verified on the official site or any source and should be confirmed on arrival.
nara_mikasa_kanko_kaikan.notes: Mikasa Kanko Kaikan sits at the foot of Wakakusayama in the heart of Nara Park, a short walk east of the city center toward Kasuga Taisha. It is a long-running tourist hall that pairs a ground-floor souvenir shop with sit-down dining spread across two floors — table seating downs

chef_bio.background: Mikasa Kanko Kaikan sits at the foot of Wakakusayama in the heart of Nara Park, a short walk east of the city center toward Kasuga Taisha. It is a long-running tourist hall that pairs a ground-floor souvenir shop with sit-down dining spread across two floors — table seating downstairs and a mix of tables and tatami-mat rooms upstairs — making it a common stop for school groups and sightseeing travelers exploring the deer park.
chef_bio.specialty: Hearty Nara-style set meals and bento: the Sōhei (warrior-monk) bento, tonkatsu and Nanto set meals, kamameshi, teppanyaki sets, katsu curry and hamburg plates, alongside a Buddhist-vegetarian (shōjin) set. Bundles of deer crackers (shika-senbei) are sold out front for feeding the park's free-roaming deer.

anecdotes.text: The hall is named after Mikasayama (the older name for Wakakusayama, the grassy hill it sits beneath), the same mountain that lent its name to Nara's famous Mikasa sweet — a dorayaki-style confection whose shape evokes the rounded mountain.
It functions as a one-stop tourist rest house — souvenirs and packaged Nara sweets downstairs, full meals upstairs, and deer crackers for sale at the entrance for visitors feeding the park deer.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official restaurant page lists the set meals (Sohei bento, tonkatsu, Nanto set, kamameshi, teppanyaki, katsu curry, hamburg, shojin vegetarian) and the Wakakusayama-foot address (雑司町933). MAFF traditional-foods page documents the Mikasa confection named after the mountain.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu is dominated by deep-fried and wheat-based dishes (tonkatsu, katsu curry, hamburg, udon) served in a shared high-volume kitchen; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese set meals and bento are served, which in Japan typically use wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free seasoning is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A Buddhist-vegetarian (shōjin) set is offered, but it is prepared in the same kitchen as meat and fish dishes and its dashi/seasoning ingredients are not disclosed, so vegan suitability and cross-contact cannot be confirmed.
