positives.text: A dedicated Buddhist-vegetarian (shōjin) set meal is available on the regular menu, giving plant-based diners a starting point to ask about.

cultural_comfort.note: A large, tourist-facing dining hall and souvenir shop in Nara Park where ordering is straightforward by pointing at set-meal photos; basic greetings are enough, though detailed dietary questions may need patience or a translation app.

nara_kasuga_taisha_cafe_shop_.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation found. The menu centers on wheat-based items: Miwa sōmen / nyūmen and ramen are wheat noodles, pancakes and cookies contain wheat flour, and there is no dedicated fryer or allergen handling documented. Not celiac-safe.
nara_kasuga_taisha_cafe_shop_.vegan_detail: No confirmed vegan items. The documented soft serve flavors (matcha, matcha-milk, chocolate, mango-milk, etc.) are all dairy-based, and meal sets use rice/sōmen typically with fish dashi. Despite a claim that a vegan soft serve is offered, no source I checked lists a ヴィーガン/植物性 (plant-based) item, so a plant-based eater would need to ask directly.
nara_kasuga_taisha_cafe_shop_.hours_raw: 10:30–17:00 (L.O. 16:30); rurubu lists 10:00–17:00 (L.O. 16:30). Follows the Kasuga Taisha National Treasure Hall schedule.
nara_kasuga_taisha_cafe_shop_.notes: The space is built to carry the feeling of Kasuga's primeval forest indoors: its counter is fashioned from a Kasuga cedar that grew on the mountain and was felled by a lightning strike in the Showa era, and other wooden fittings are made from nagi, a tree designated a natural mon

chef_bio.origin: Opened in autumn 2015 alongside the renovated National Treasure Hall (Kokuhoden) of Kasuga Taisha, this cafe and shop sits on the first floor of the museum building within the shrine's sacred grounds in Nara Park.
chef_bio.background: The space is built to carry the feeling of Kasuga's primeval forest indoors: its counter is fashioned from a Kasuga cedar that grew on the mountain and was felled by a lightning strike in the Showa era, and other wooden fittings are made from nagi, a tree designated a natural monument. A display of an 800-year-old cedar stump anchors the room.
chef_bio.philosophy: To let visitors to the shrine taste Nara's local produce and feel the atmosphere of the sacred Kasuga mountain forest within the cafe itself.
chef_bio.specialty: Soft serve made with Nara-grown matcha is the signature, offered in five flavors, alongside sweets like black-honey-and-kinako pancakes with warabi mochi and the Shiki Gozen seasonal set pairing Nara rice bowls with Miwa somen.

anecdotes.text: The cafe's counter table is cut from a cedar that once stood on Mount Kasuga and was struck by lightning during the Showa period, having been stored at the old treasure house before being repurposed here.
Original goods and confections are themed on cats found depicted in the scabbards of national-treasure swords held by the shrine.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: smartmagazine confirms every detail: Oct 2015 opening with the renovated Kokuhoden, the counter from a Mt. Mikasa (Kasuga) cedar struck by lightning in the Showa era, the 800-year-old stump (with a ~500-year-old pebble embedded), nagi natural-monument wood, five matcha soft-serve flavors, kinako pancakes (970yen), Shiki Gozen with Miwa somen (1,600yen), and cat goods drawn from national-treasure sword scabbards.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Soft serve flavors documented are dairy-based (matcha-milk, chocolate-milk, mango-milk), so plant-based options are not confirmed and any would share equipment with dairy.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed museum cafe inside a major shrine's National Treasure Hall, used to tourists and easy to order at by pointing, though staff English may be limited so a translation app helps.

nara_aonocafe.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination and no GF accommodation is documented. The base food is rice (onigiri), and a plain-salt onigiri (こだわりの塩) exists, but the lunch sets come with a rolled egg, a hearty pork soup (tonjiru) that almost certainly contains wheat-based miso/seasoning, and fillings such as seared cheese-mentaiko, tuna mayo, and roast beef that may use soy sauce or other wheat-containing seasonings. There is no mention of dedicated GF handling or cross-contamination control. A celiac diner would need to ask in detail and likely cannot eat the standard set safely.
nara_aonocafe.vegan_detail: Not vegan-oriented. The signature lunches center on fish, meat, and dairy fillings (tuna mayo, mentaiko, seared cheese, prosciutto with cream cheese, roast beef) and include a rolled egg and a pork-based soup. A plain-salt or kombu onigiri could in principle be vegan if ordered à la carte, but the set meals are not, fish dashi is likely in the soup, and no vegan menu is documented. A vegan would need to ask whether individual non-animal onigiri can be ordered separately.
nara_aonocafe.notes: [Mom & Pop] A photogenic onigiri café that opened on March 25, 2024 in the Koinokubo area northwest of central Nara. The shop is built around handmade rice balls and a relaxed, welcoming lunch atmosphere.

chef_bio.background: A photogenic onigiri café that opened on March 25, 2024 in the Koinokubo area northwest of central Nara. The shop is built around handmade rice balls and a relaxed, welcoming lunch atmosphere.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated draw is offering unique rice-ball varieties you can't find elsewhere, served generously and affordably for a satisfying everyday lunch.
chef_bio.specialty: Onigiri lunch sets: diners choose three rice balls from around fifteen original fillings. The playful menu splits into an 'Ao' (blue) line of classics like tuna-mayo and mentaiko, and a 'Shiro' (white) line of creative choices such as seared cheese-mentaiko, house-made roast beef, kombu, and prosciutto with cream cheese. Each set comes with a generous, vegetable-packed pork soup, a rolled egg, and small sides, with takeout also available.

anecdotes.text: Opened on March 25, 2024 and quickly drew attention as a 'photogenic onigiri shop,' with a full lunch set built around three chosen rice balls and a hearty pork soup offered around the 1,000-yen mark.
Visitors describe a warm, busy little café with the rice-ball sets praised as filling yet never monotonous thanks to the vegetable-forward pork soup.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: par-ple confirms the Mar 25 2024 opening, the photogenic-onigiri framing, choose-3-of-~15 fillings, Ao (tuna-mayo, mentaiko) and Shiro (seared cheese-mentaiko, roast beef, kombu) lines, pork soup and ~1,000yen sets with takeout. narameshi corroborates the filling, varied sets.

positives.text: The core dish is rice-based onigiri, and a simple salt onigiri (こだわりの塩) and kombu onigiri are on the filling list, so plain rice-ball options exist for diners avoiding meat or fish if ordered carefully.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly local lunch café where a smile and a little basic Japanese go a long way; the menu is simple (pick your rice-ball fillings), so a foreign student can manage comfortably even with limited Japanese.

nara_hibi_murakami.gf_detail: This is a wheat bakery whose entire product line is built on domestic wheat flour (plus rice and other grains), so it is not suitable for celiacs or anyone avoiding gluten. No gluten-free products are documented.
nara_hibi_murakami.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is advertised. Documented items include shokupan, melon pan with almonds, anko-and-butter, and curry pan, several of which clearly contain dairy/egg. Some simple hard-crust breads may be free of animal products, but ingredients are not published, so a vegan diner would need to ask item by item.
nara_hibi_murakami.notes: [2026-08-19] Former official domain hibimurakami.com has lapsed and now serves an Indonesian gambling site; the link was removed. Verify the business is still trading. [Mom & Pop] A small bakery in Nara's quiet Kitamachi (Horen-cho) district, a short walk north of Kintetsu Nara Station along the Saho River. It was founded by the Murakami family to be a neighborhood bread shop rooted in their home city of Nara.

chef_bio.background: A small bakery in Nara's quiet Kitamachi (Horen-cho) district, a short walk north of Kintetsu Nara Station along the Saho River. It was founded by the Murakami family to be a neighborhood bread shop rooted in their home city of Nara.
chef_bio.philosophy: To make gentle, everyday bread that children and elderly customers alike can enjoy, kept at approachable prices and convenient hours, using domestic wheat and local Nara ingredients such as Yamato tea and Nara-grown rice so the bakery stays tied to its hometown.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature 'Hibi no Shokupan' (daily milk-style loaf) made from a proprietary blend of domestic wheat and Nara rice, with a soft, chewy crumb that is faintly sweet eaten plain and crisp-edged when toasted. Other beloved items include 'Yamato-cha to Azuki' (organic Nara green tea and sweet adzuki swirl), a baked-not-fried vegetable curry pan, the almond-and-sugar 'Sunrise' melon pan, and an anko-and-butter roll.

anecdotes.text: The owner is described talking about bread with sparkling eyes, wanting the shop to walk alongside the community's daily life, which is the spirit behind the name 'Hibi' (everyday).
The curry pan is filled with house-made curry of onion and carrot and is baked rather than deep-fried so it appeals to all ages.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: par-ple confirms owner Murakami's 'sparkling eyes' community ethos, use of domestic wheat, Nara rice and Yamato tea, the chewy Hibi no Shokupan, Yamato-cha & azuki, baked (not fried) curry pan, Sunrise melon pan, anko-butter roll, and the ~8-min-walk Kitamachi/Saho-river location.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a flour-based bakery where every product is made with domestic wheat, so there is pervasive wheat/gluten throughout the kitchen and no gluten-free options exist.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Documented breads include dairy and egg items (milk-style shokupan, almond melon pan, anko-and-butter), so animal ingredients and shared surfaces are common; no vegan-specific handling is described.

positives.text: The bakery emphasizes domestic wheat and local Nara ingredients (Nara rice, Yamato tea), so ingredient sourcing is transparent and locally focused.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny neighborhood bakery where you point at what you want and pay at the counter, so a foreign student can shop comfortably with little or no Japanese, though staff are unlikely to speak English.

nara_u_s_kitchen.gf_detail: This is a fresh-pasta specialist where essentially every dish is wheat-based (tagliatelle, linguine, pappardelle, spaghetti, penne). There is no documented gluten-free menu, no gluten-free pasta, and no celiac accommodation. Not suitable for those who must avoid gluten.
nara_u_s_kitchen.vegan_detail: An Italian pasta house built around cream sauces, meat sauce, bacon, baby scallop, smoked chicken and shrimp dishes. A plain tomato-sauce pasta or basil pesto (ジェノベーゼ) may be the only meatless option, but no dish is confirmed dairy-free or vegan, and there is no documented vegan menu. Vegans would need to call ahead and likely find very little.
nara_u_s_kitchen.hours_raw: Lunch 11:00-14:30, Dinner 17:00-20:30 (last entry); closed Sundays; dinner closed on the third Monday.
nara_u_s_kitchen.notes: [Mom & Pop] A snug pasta room tucked into Nara's old Kitamachi quarter, a short walk north from the Kintetsu station amid the nostalgic streetscape near the Higashimuki shopping arcade. It has been a quiet local favorite for years rather than a tourist stop.

chef_bio.background: A snug pasta room tucked into Nara's old Kitamachi quarter, a short walk north from the Kintetsu station amid the nostalgic streetscape near the Higashimuki shopping arcade. It has been a quiet local favorite for years rather than a tourist stop.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner keeps the focus deliberately narrow, stating that this is a pasta specialist that serves pasta and nothing else, letting the noodles and sauces carry the meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Fresh house-made pasta is the heart of the menu, built around three carefully chosen shapes: tagliatelle (an egg-rich ribbon a bit like kishimen), linguine with a firm bite and faint sweetness, and wide pappardelle. The kitchen turns out a long list of sauces, and the baby-scallop cream pasta is a standout regulars come back for.

anecdotes.text: A longtime regular writes that they stumbled on this pasta specialist years ago and it became their go-to, praising the chewy tagliatelle in baby-scallop cream sauce.
The restaurant's own site sums up its identity bluntly: as a pasta specialty shop, there is nothing on the menu but pasta.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: naralunch confirms the pasta-only concept, the three fresh shapes (tagliatelle likened to kishimen, linguine, pappardelle), the chewy baby-scallop cream pasta, and the Higashimuki-kita arcade / north-of-Kintetsu-Nara location (fresh pasta +220yen over dried). No owner name is given.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire menu is built on house-made wheat pasta, so flour is central to the kitchen; there is no gluten-free preparation or separate workflow documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Sauces lean heavily on cream, meat sauce, bacon, scallop, chicken and shrimp, so meat- and dairy-free cooking is not a focus and shared pots are likely.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally loved neighborhood pasta room where menus and service are in Japanese, so a few words of Japanese or a translation app will make ordering smoother for a foreign student.

nara_nara_kitamachi_shokudo_i.gf_detail: No gluten-free program. This is an Italian/Western canteen built around pasta, fried items (フリット), and rice plates, so wheat is pervasive and there is no celiac-safe handling. The chef is known for adjusting dishes to customer requests, so you could ask, but cross-contamination cannot be assured in a kitchen this small.
nara_nara_kitamachi_shokudo_i.vegan_detail: Not a vegan/vegetarian destination — the menu centers on meat and fish mains (fried chicken breast, grilled pork, deep-fried horse mackerel). The owner does customize dishes and asks diners about dislikes, so a vegetable-forward plate might be possible by request, but no documented vegan offering exists. House-made non-alcoholic sangria is one plant-based item noted.
nara_nara_kitamachi_shokudo_i.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, home-style Italian and Western canteen tucked on the second floor of a building in Nara's historic Kitamachi district, near Nara Women's University. Run by an owner who goes by Sadayan with one part-time helper, it sits along the route east from Kintetsu Nara Station thr

chef_bio.background: A small, home-style Italian and Western canteen tucked on the second floor of a building in Nara's historic Kitamachi district, near Nara Women's University. Run by an owner who goes by Sadayan with one part-time helper, it sits along the route east from Kintetsu Nara Station through the Higashimuki and Hanashiba shopping streets, marked by a wooden sign painted with black cats.
chef_bio.philosophy: The Italian name means 'the family's smile,' reflecting the owner's stated wish to meet many customers' happy, satisfied faces each day. The kitchen embraces flexibility, adjusting sauces and ingredients to individual tastes and inviting requests.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily-changing one-plate lunch sets (around 850-900 yen) with a rotating main such as fried chicken breast, grilled pork shoulder, or deep-fried horse mackerel, served with a generous portion of rice, assorted sides, and fruit; pasta dishes and a teppan Neapolitan are also signatures, alongside house-made non-alcoholic sangria.

anecdotes.text: The shop keeps the spirit of a relaxed 'home drinking' spot where you can come alone for a single drink or gather with friends and family, and it is known for keeping cats around, adding to its casual, family feel.
A diner came away with the strong impression that the chef genuinely loves cooking, noting the kitchen will tweak dishes to suit the customer.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: burakita confirms owner nickname Sadayan, the 'family's smile' meaning, the 2F location near Nara Women's University with a black-cat parent-and-child wooden sign, the ~850yen one-plate lunch (three main choices, sides, rice/baguette), pasta lunch, non-alcoholic homemade sangria, and the cat-friendly home-drinking atmosphere.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff ask diners about dislikes and will adjust sauces and ingredients to suit individual tastes, and the menu can be customized on request.

positives.text: The owner welcomes customer requests and can accommodate dietary preferences or specific dish requests.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, student-friendly owner-run canteen near Nara Women's University where ordering and chatting will go most smoothly in Japanese, though the relaxed family atmosphere is welcoming to all.

nara_bocarroz.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core menu is craft hamburgers on house-made brioche/wheat buns, and there is no documented gluten-free option or celiac handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_bocarroz.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The concept centers on hand-chopped beef patties, house-made bacon and smoked brisket, plus cheese; Spanish tapas also lean meat/seafood. No documented vegan or vegetarian dishes.
nara_bocarroz.hours_raw: Tue–Sun & holidays 11:30–15:00, 18:00–20:00 (lunch until 15:00; dinner noted as starting at 17:00 or 18:00). Ends when sold out. Closed Mon.
nara_bocarroz.notes: [Mom & Pop] BOCARROZ is a craft-burger & tapas bar that the owner opened independently in Kitamachi's Hanashibachō in April 2021, after closing his Spanish restaurant "Gentry" in Nara in March 2021. Drawing on his background as a former Spanish-cuisine chef, he has established his own style of pairing hamburgers with Spanish small plates.

chef_bio.origin: 店名『ボカロス』は、スペイン語で『ボカディージョ（サンドイッチ）』のボカと、米料理を意味する『アロス（arroz）』を組み合わせた造語です。
chef_bio.background: ボカロスは、奈良市内でスペイン料理店『Gentry（ジェントリー）』を営んでいた店主が、2021年3月に同店を閉め、2021年4月にきたまち・花芝町で独立開業したクラフトバーガー＆タパスバルです。元スペイン料理シェフの経歴を生かし、ハンバーガーにスペインの小皿料理を組み合わせた独自のスタイルを打ち出しています。
chef_bio.philosophy: バンズを毎朝店で焼き、ベーコン・ブリスケット・ソースまで自家製にこだわる、手作り主体のクラフト志向。夜はハンバーガーに加えてスペインのタパスやワイン・カクテルが楽しめ、ランチとは異なるバル的な雰囲気になります。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板はカルニータスバーガー。豚肩肉をオレンジとスパイスで低温コンフィ風にじっくり火入れし、ほろほろと柔らかく仕上げた一品で、丼スタイルでも提供されます。ほかにベーコンチーズバーガー、ダブルチーズバーガー、BBQチーズバーガーなど。バンズは自家製ブリオッシュ、パティは手切り（ハンドチョップ）のビーフ、ベーコンやスモークブリスケット、各種ソースまで店で手作りしています。自家製コーラやジンジャーエールも提供。

anecdotes.text: 店名『ボカロス（BOCARROZ）』はスペイン語のボカディージョ（サンドイッチ）の『ボカ』と、米料理を意味する『アロス（arroz）』を掛け合わせた造語。
店主は元スペイン料理店『Gentry』のオーナーシェフで、2021年3月に同店を閉店、同年4月にボカロスを開業した。
看板のカルニータスバーガーは豚肩肉をオレンジとスパイスで低温コンフィ風に火入れし、丼でも提供される。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet states the name is a coinage of Spanish Bocadillo (ボカ) + Arroz (rice) and that the ex-Gentry chef restarted as a burger bar. kojita gives the dates (Gentry closed 2021/3/26, BOCARROZ opened 2021/4/1) and the all-house-made line-up. narakko confirms the 花芝町 craft-burger + tapas concept, hand-cut beef patty, and the signature carnitas burger (1,500yen) served also over rice.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 18-seat chef-run burger and tapas bar where a few Japanese greetings and pointing at the menu will carry you through comfortably, though staff may not speak much English.

nara_sahha.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free program. The signature dish is couscous, which is wheat-based semolina pasta and unsafe for celiacs. However, some naturally gluten-free items exist: falafel (chickpea), shakshuka (a tomato/vegetable stew), and rice-based kebsa/biryani. Cross-contamination is not addressed in any source, and harissa/spice blends and sauces have unverified ingredients. A gluten-free diner would need to ask the owner directly about each dish.
nara_sahha.vegan_detail: The restaurant explicitly offers some vegan-appropriate and vegetarian dishes. Documented plant-based options include falafel (chickpea, ~¥1,300) and shakshuka (Tunisian vegetable/tomato stew, ~¥1,200), and the kitchen emphasizes fresh vegetables (cabbage, chickpeas, dates, radish, zucchini, onion, carrot). It is not a fully vegan restaurant — couscous and kebsa dishes are prepared with lamb or chicken. Confirm egg-free preparation of shakshuka, which can sometimes include egg, directly with the owner.
nara_sahha.hours_raw: 11:30–20:00 (some sources list split hours of 11:30–15:00 / 17:00–20:30). Closed Fridays; some sources also note Mondays and irregular closures.
nara_sahha.notes: SAHHA is a Tunisian and North African restaurant tucked inside a renovated traditional Japanese house (kominka) in the Kitamachi district of Nara, near Nara Women's University. It opened in August 2021 and is one of very few places in Nara — and rare even nationwide in Japan — se

chef_bio.background: SAHHA is a Tunisian and North African restaurant tucked inside a renovated traditional Japanese house (kominka) in the Kitamachi district of Nara, on a corner northwest of Nara Women's University. It opened in August 2021 and is one of very few places in Nara — and rare even nationwide in Japan — serving authentic Tunisian home cooking. The owner, Madani Imed, from Tunisia, runs the place together with his Japanese partner, with his mother's Tataouine-style home cooking at the heart of the kitchen.
chef_bio.philosophy: Every dish on the menu is halal, so Muslim travelers can eat freely, and the kitchen leans heavily on fresh vegetables — cabbage, chickpeas, dates, radish, zucchini, onion and carrot — giving vegetarians and vegans some honest options too.
chef_bio.specialty: Couscous is the signature: the traditional couscous (around ¥1,400) is built on the world's smallest pasta soaking up a tomato-based broth simmered with root vegetables and lamb, finished with a hint of raisin sweetness. Other beloved dishes include kebsa (an Arab-style spiced long-grain rice biryani with lamb or chicken, described as milder than its Indian counterpart), shakshuka (a Tunisian tomato-and-vegetable stew), and falafel made from chickpeas. Homemade harissa chili paste, baklava, and Arab coffee round out the table.

anecdotes.text: The traditional couscous is said to taste richer the more you chew it, the tiny pasta grains soaking up a lamb-and-root-vegetable broth with a faint sweetness of raisin.
The dining space is a restored kominka with tatami rooms dressed in Middle Eastern textiles, where guests remove their shoes and sit low in a North African mood inside an old Nara house.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: naralunch confirms the Aug 2021 opening, the renovated kominka with tatami seating, halal cuisine, and couscous (1,400yen), shakshuka, chicken kebsa and falafel. Nara Hitomachi University (nhmu.jp) and the official site (sahha.jp) give the owner's name, MADANI IMED from Tunisia, run with a Japanese partner, with the owner's mother cooking Tataouine-style home food. nara-gourmet confirms all dishes are halal with vegan options.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The entire menu is prepared to halal standards, which means strict attention to what goes into each dish, and the owner runs the kitchen personally — making it practical to ask about ingredients directly.

positives.text: Documented vegetable-forward and chickpea-based options exist, including falafel and shakshuka, alongside an emphasis on fresh produce.
Naturally gluten-free choices such as falafel, shakshuka and rice-based kebsa are on the menu, though cross-contamination is not documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A small owner-run place where the Tunisian proprietor is used to international guests and Muslim diners, so a friendly greeting and a few words about your dietary needs will be warmly received.

nara_kaya_cafe_naramachi_ten.gf_detail: No gluten-free claims are documented. The signature tofu tiramisu and other sweets (pancakes, parfaits) typically contain wheat-based components (sponge/biscuit, flour), and savory items like omelette rice are not GF. There is no published allergen information or dedicated gluten-free preparation, so a celiac traveler must ask directly and should not assume safety.
nara_kaya_cafe_naramachi_ten.vegan_detail: Although the desserts are tofu-based and marketed as healthy, they are not described as vegan. The tiramisu is "creamy" in a mascarpone style and the menu includes items like strawberry milk and omelette rice, indicating dairy and egg use. No vegan labeling is published, so vegans must confirm ingredients in person.
nara_kaya_cafe_naramachi_ten.notes: A specialty tofu-sweets café in the historic Naramachi neighborhood, about a 10-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station and minutes from Sarusawa Pond. The Naramachi location opened in early 2023 (pre-opening in late January, with a February 1, 2023 start), joining the brand's pre

chef_bio.background: A specialty tofu-sweets café in the historic Naramachi neighborhood (Tsurufukuin-cho), about a 10-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station and minutes from Sarusawa Pond. The Naramachi location opened in early 2023 (pre-opening on weekends in late January, with the grand opening in February 2023), joining the brand's popular sibling shops in Osaka's Nakazakicho and Kobe's Motomachi.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café centers on 'guilt-free,' health-conscious sweets made with tofu that are described as creamy and indulgent without tasting of tofu.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade tofu tiramisu served in a small wooden box, offered in flavors such as cocoa, matcha, hojicha, black sesame, mango, and a seasonal fresh-strawberry version ('Ichigo kaoru tofu tiramisu'). The menu also features parfaits, pancakes, an 'Angel Strawberry Milk' drink, and savory omelette rice.

anecdotes.text: The tofu tiramisu is presented in a stylish wooden box, making it both photogenic and healthy, which has made it especially popular.
Local coverage framed the shop around saying goodbye to guilt by eating seasonal tiramisu made from tofu.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: narakko confirms the Naramachi (Tsurufukuin-cho) tofu-tiramisu specialty, the wooden-box presentation, flavors (cocoa, matcha, hojicha, black sesame, mango, strawberry) at 550yen, and healthy/creamy framing. goguynet confirms the late-Jan-2023 pre-opening with a February grand opening and the popular sibling shops in Osaka Nakazakicho and Kobe Motomachi (12-seat interior, omelette rice).

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly local sweets café where a foreign student can comfortably order with a few basic Japanese words and pointing at the photo menu, though staff may have limited English.

nara_yamato_jika_baisen_ouza_.gf_detail: This is a coffee shop, not a kitchen geared to dietary needs. Black coffee itself is naturally gluten-free, but the food offered (hot dogs) is wheat-based bread, and no gluten-free food or celiac-safe handling is documented. Treat it as a place for a drink rather than a safe gluten-free meal.
nara_yamato_jika_baisen_ouza_.vegan_detail: Black coffee is the core offering and is plant-based, but no plant milk or vegan menu is documented; food items such as the hot dog are not vegan. Suitable only if you stick to black coffee; confirm milk options on site.
nara_yamato_jika_baisen_ouza_.hours_raw: 10:00–19:00. Closed Mondays (also closed during Obon, year-end/New Year, and some holidays).
nara_yamato_jika_baisen_ouza_.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop is run by Mr. Shirai, who took up coffee roasting after retiring and became absorbed in its depth and complexity, eventually opening this self-roasting coffee shop in the quiet Koi-no-kubo residential district of Nara.

chef_bio.background: The shop is run by Mr. Shirai (白井祥雅), who took up coffee roasting after retiring and became absorbed in its depth and complexity, eventually opening this self-roasting coffee shop (established 2018) in the quiet Koi-no-kubo (恋の窪) residential district of Nara.
chef_bio.philosophy: To help each customer find the coffee truly suited to their taste and to enjoy fresh, aromatic specialty coffee, while creating a relaxed gathering place for the neighborhood. Green beans are checked for defects before roasting and hand-picked afterward for quality.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted specialty coffee (around 20 varieties sold by weight from the display shelves), with a signature 'Sakura Blend' that is balanced with fruity notes and evokes the Saho River cherry blossoms nearby; beans are roasted in-house on a 1kg roaster, and food includes hot dogs and cake sets.

anecdotes.text: First-time visitors are offered a complimentary tasting, and buying 200g or more of beans comes with a free cup of coffee — small touches reflecting the shop's wish to be welcoming.
The shop sits near the cherry-tree-lined banks of the Saho River, a peaceful setting that inspired its 'Sakura' blend.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ouzacoffee.com (official) confirms the self-roasting concept, 1kg roaster, defect-checking and hand-picking, Koi-no-kubo location near the Saho River, and hot dog/cake-set food. naraliving.com profiles owner 白井祥雅 (age ~69), who began roasting after retirement, and the fruity Sakura Blend among ~20 beans.

positives.text: Black self-roasted coffee is the focus, brewed cup by cup, so a plain cup of coffee is naturally free of gluten and animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run neighborhood roastery where Japanese is the working language; a friendly point-and-smile spot for a coffee, but do not expect English menus or service.

nara_unakiku_nara_honten.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature unagi is grilled and finished with a tare made from wheat-based soy sauce (Tenno Shoyu) and mirin, so the core dish contains gluten. No dedicated gluten-free menu, preparation, or accommodation is documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_unakiku_nara_honten.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. This is a dedicated freshwater-eel (unagi) specialist; the entire menu centers on grilled live eel. No plant-based dishes are documented.
nara_unakiku_nara_honten.hours_raw: Lunch 11:00-14:45 (last entry), Dinner 17:00-19:00 (last entry); last order around 18:30. Closed Tuesdays. Year-end/New Year closures and a modified New Year's menu apply.
nara_unakiku_nara_honten.notes: Unakiku is a dedicated eel restaurant born from Kikusuiro, a celebrated ryotei founded in 1891 (Meiji 24) and now a registered tangible cultural property, set directly in front of the first torii gate of Kasuga Taisha shrine. For more than 130 years the house has welcomed disting

chef_bio.background: Unakiku is a dedicated eel restaurant born from Kikusuiro, a celebrated ryotei founded in 1891 (Meiji 24) and now a registered tangible cultural property, set directly in front of the first torii gate of Kasuga Taisha shrine. For more than 130 years the house has welcomed distinguished guests, and Unakiku carries that hospitality into a focused eel specialty.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant frames eating eel as part of a pilgrimage ritual, building on the local custom of enjoying unagi after visiting Kasuga Taisha, and aims to connect people through eel cuisine.
chef_bio.specialty: Edo-style unagi: live eels are filleted to order, white-grilled, thoroughly steamed, then charcoal-grilled with the house tare. Signature dishes include the classic unagi-don and the ainose-don, which pairs plain white-grilled eel (shirayaki) with tare-glazed eel in one bowl. The tare blends pure additive-free Tenno Shoyu soy sauce (brewed with Fuji spring water) and traditional hon-mirin, and the rice is exclusively Niigata Uonuma Koshihikari grown for the restaurant by a partner farmer.

anecdotes.text: Unakiku grew out of the long-standing local custom of eating eel after worshipping at Kasuga Taisha, positioning itself in front of the shrine's first torii gate as part of Nara's food-culture pilgrimage experience.
Its parent house, Kikusuiro, has served guests for over 130 years and is a registered tangible cultural property dating to 1891 (Meiji 24).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kikusuiro.com/unakiku (official) confirms the Kikusuiro parentage founded Meiji 24 (1891) as a registered tangible cultural property, the first-torii location, the aim of making post-shrine eel a Nara custom, the fillet-to-order/white-grill/steam/charcoal-grill method, the Tenno Shoyu (Fuji spring water) + hon-mirin (Kanasugu Brewery) tare, and Niigata Uonuma Koshihikari rice from partner farmer Ishizaka.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature tare is made by blending pure Tenno Shoyu soy sauce with hon-mirin; standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the eel glaze contains gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a dedicated eel restaurant; effectively every dish is built around grilled freshwater eel, so there is no plant-based mainline and shared grill/tare make it unsuitable for vegans.

cultural_comfort.note: An upscale eel restaurant inside a historic ryotei property where reservations and basic Japanese dining etiquette help; a foreign student can manage with a polite "konnichiwa," a reservation, and a translation app, but it is a special-occasion splurge rather than a casual drop-in.

nara_authentic_table_tavern.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. This is a casual French/yoshoku restaurant whose menu includes sauces, homemade ham, soup curry and charcoal-grilled dishes; flour-based sauces and wheat are common in this cuisine, so it is not celiac-safe without direct confirmation. A celiac diner must ask the kitchen about every dish.
nara_authentic_table_tavern.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. The kitchen does source seasonal Yamato vegetables from Nara and grills vegetables such as broccoli, but the menu centers on charcoal-grilled meats, fresh fish, homemade Yamato-pork ham and dairy-based French preparations. There may be vegetable side dishes, but no confirmed plant-only mains; a vegan diner should call ahead and ask.
nara_authentic_table_tavern.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Sun: 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:30) & 17:30-21:00 (L.O. 20:30); Fri, Sat & day before public holiday: 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:30) & 17:30-22:00 (L.O. 21:30). Closed Wednesday (subject to change).
nara_authentic_table_tavern.notes: A casual French dining room set on Sanjo-dori, the historic street running between Nara Station and Kasuga Taisha Shrine, in a warm interior of natural-wood tones meant for relaxed special occasions.

chef_bio.background: A casual French dining room set on Sanjo-dori, the historic street running between Nara Station and Kasuga Taisha Shrine, in a warm interior of natural-wood tones meant for relaxed special occasions.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen aims to honor the natural flavor of its ingredients, sourcing seasonal Yamato vegetables and premium produce and using special sauces and spices only as refined accents rather than to mask the food.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled cooking is the heart of the kitchen, built around carefully chosen ingredients from Nara and Hokkaido. Signature plates include charcoal-grilled steak and vegetables, fresh charcoal-grilled fish, a house specialty soup curry, and homemade ham made from Yamato pork (served with onion sauce), all paired with an extensive sommelier-curated wine list.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant hosts wine-pairing evenings and occasional live guitar performances ('FIESTA'), doubling as a relaxed evening venue.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: noborioji.com/tavern (official) confirms the Sanjo-dori casual-French concept, charcoal-grill cooking with Nara/Hokkaido ingredients, sommelier wine list, monthly wine-pairing courses and 'FIESTA' live-guitar nights. Tabelog and nara-gourmet.com corroborate the soup curry, charcoal-grilled fresh fish and house-made Yamato-pork ham with onion sauce.

positives.text: Sources seasonal Yamato vegetables from Nara and offers charcoal-grilled vegetable dishes such as broccoli, so some plant-forward options exist on the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A multilingual (English) menu is available and the staff are used to guests, so a foreign student can order comfortably; web and phone reservations are accepted.

nara_bakery_gen.gf_detail: This is a conventional wheat-flour bakery; the owners blend several types of wheat flour for their breads, and signature items (cream pan, milk bread, focaccia, kouign-amann) are all wheat-based. There is no gluten-free offering and no measures against cross-contamination documented. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.
nara_bakery_gen.vegan_detail: Breads documented include custard-cream pan (eggs/dairy), butter-rich kouign-amann, and milk bread, so dairy/eggs/butter are common. One item noted is an egg-free milk bread, but it is not described as vegan (likely still contains dairy/butter), and no vegan range is advertised. Not a vegan destination; a vegan traveler would need to ask about specific loaves and assume most contain animal products.
nara_bakery_gen.hours_raw: 9:00–18:00 (closes early when bread sells out). Closed every Monday and Friday.
nara_bakery_gen.notes: [Mom & Pop] BAKERY GEN is a small neighborhood bakery run by a husband-and-wife team in the Sakyo residential district of northern Nara, set among the Heijo New Town housing estates. The couple bake roughly 40 kinds of bread by hand each day and pride themselves on being close to their custo

chef_bio.background: BAKERY GEN is a small neighborhood bakery run by a husband-and-wife team in the Sakyo residential district of northern Nara, set among the Heijo-Sakyo (Takanohara) housing estates. The couple bake roughly 40 kinds of bread by hand each day and pride themselves on being close to their customers, often turning conversations at the counter into new products on the shelves.
chef_bio.philosophy: They describe themselves as a bakery that stays close to the community, adjusting the blend of several wheat flours to suit each bread and recipe, drawing on years of accumulated technique, and developing new breads from customer feedback.
chef_bio.specialty: Their best-known item is the cream pan, filled with rich hand-strained custard cream made fresh to pair with their dough. Other favorites include a salted potato focaccia, an egg-free fluffy milk bread using quality fresh cream, and a buttery kouign-amann.

anecdotes.text: The name GEN comes from a beloved family dog the owner lived with as a child; the shop carries the wish that the family can always stay together.
The bakery is woven into the life of the surrounding Heijo-Sakyo housing estate, profiled as part of a feature on the relationship between bread shops and danchi communities.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: bakery-gen.com (official) confirms the husband-and-wife shop in Nara-shi Sakyo (Laurel Square Takanohara), ~40 breads daily, the cream-pan flagship, salted-potato focaccia, egg-free milk bread and kouign-amann, and the flour-blending philosophy. weeeeks.jp / orusuma2 confirm the GEN name comes from the owner's childhood family dog. The UR danchi feature places the shop in the Heijo-Sakyo estate.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Conventional bakery that blends multiple wheat flours for its breads; flour is used throughout, so cross-contamination is unavoidable and there is no gluten-free production.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Breads commonly use eggs, dairy, custard cream, and butter; no vegan line is advertised and shared equipment/surfaces would contact animal-derived ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood bakery in a residential danchi far from the tourist center; little to no English, so point at what you want and pay at the counter — straightforward even with no Japanese.

nara_nagi_no_ki.gf_detail: This is an Italian kitchen built around pasta and Western dishes, so wheat is central and there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation; not suitable for celiacs. The kakigori may be naturally wheat-light but no gluten-free handling is documented.
nara_nagi_no_ki.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. It is a creative Italian restaurant likely using meat, fish, dairy and eggs, and the signature kakigori use syrups, umeboshi paste and a tomato-and-sour-cream version that is not vegan. A vegan diner would need to ask directly about any plant-based options.
nara_nagi_no_ki.hours_raw: Italian: 11:30- (L.O. 14:00), 18:00- (L.O. 20:30), dinner by reservation. Kakigori served irregularly (mainly summer) on days when dinner reservations are not taken; check Instagram for dates/times.
nara_nagi_no_ki.notes: [Mom & Pop] The chef trained at prestigious Tokyo hotels and restaurants before opening this small Italian cafe in 2017 in Takabatake-cho, his wife's hometown, in a quiet corner of central Nara near the Nara Hotel.

chef_bio.origin: Tokyo fine-dining background; settled in Nara.
chef_bio.background: The chef trained at prestigious Tokyo hotels and restaurants before opening this small Italian cafe in 2017 in Takabatake-cho, his wife's hometown, in a quiet corner of central Nara near the Nara Hotel.
chef_bio.philosophy: He frames the shaved ice in light of Nara's long history of worshipping the guardian deity of ice since the Heijo-kyo era, and treats kakigori as a dish rather than a sweet — building flavors with techniques borrowed from Western cooking. He offers it only irregularly, woven into the restaurant's schedule (announced via Instagram), valuing quality over convenience.
chef_bio.specialty: Creative Italian cooking using local Nara ingredients, plus a celebrated summer shaved ice. The signature is a Garden Plum Soda kakigori made from syrup pressed from the large plum tree growing on the property, layered with umeboshi paste for a sweet-tart-salty profile and a fizzing carbonated jelly at the bottom. His fine-dining background also produces savory, Italian-style kakigori such as a white-tomato version finished with basil sauce and cultured (sour) cream.

anecdotes.text: He wanted to help bring vitality to the neighborhood and took up shaved ice after receiving guidance from popular local kakigori shops, then developed his own approach using soup-like bases, salt and pepper alongside gentle sweetness.

The Garden Plum Soda kakigori is built from syrup made from the fruit of the large plum tree in the shop's own garden, with umeboshi paste adding a salty seasoning note said to help guard against summer heat exhaustion.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: rurubu.jp/andmore/article/22011 confirms the Tokyo hotel/restaurant training, the 2017 opening in the wife's hometown of Takabatake-cho, the Italian cafe in a garden mansion-style space, the ice-deity framing, the irregular Instagram-announced kakigori schedule, the Garden Plum Soda kakigori (garden plum syrup + umeboshi paste + fizzing jelly), and the savory white-tomato kakigori with basil sauce and cultured cream.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run hideaway where dinner is reservation-only and the kakigori schedule is posted irregularly on Instagram, so a foreign student will do best with some Japanese and a willingness to plan ahead.

nara_oniwa_shaveice_miracolo_2.gf_detail: A shaved ice specialist where the base is ice and house-made fruit/sugar syrups, which are inherently wheat-free. However, the shop makes no documented gluten-free claim, toppings such as konpeito candy and seasonal extras have not been verified as GF, and there is no information on a gluten-free kitchen protocol. Coeliac visitors should ask directly about each topping. Not a dedicated gluten-free establishment.
nara_oniwa_shaveice_miracolo_2.vegan_detail: Many bowls rely on dairy elements such as crème d'ange (an egg/cream sauce) and milk-based toppings, so the menu is not vegan by default. Some fruit-syrup bowls (for example the salted coconut-pineapple) may be closer to plant-based, but ingredients change daily (about five varieties offered) and no vegan labelling is documented. Vegans should ask which of the day's bowls omit dairy and egg.
nara_oniwa_shaveice_miracolo_2.hours_raw: Wed, Thu 10:00–16:00 (L.O. 15:30). Occasional special openings on other days.
nara_oniwa_shaveice_miracolo_2.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner left a career as a securities trader to pursue a long-held passion for kakigori, spending roughly a year of preparation before opening the shop in 2019 rather than launching before the quality met his standards.

chef_bio.background: The owner left a career as a securities trader to pursue a long-held passion for kakigori, spending roughly a year of preparation before opening the shop in 2019 rather than launching before the quality met their standards.
chef_bio.philosophy: Relentless quality control, with the owner describing themselves as the harshest critic of their own shaved ice; the ice is shaved for a fluffy texture and served in vessels chosen to slow melting.
chef_bio.specialty: House-made shaved ice with from-scratch syrups: a salted coconut-pineapple bowl finished with Nara konpeito candy from a long-established Nara confectioner founded in the Ansei era (mid-1800s), a 'MAX Ginger / 本気の生姜' bowl built for intense ginger umami, and a seasonal 'ミラコロいちご' using Nara's premium Koto-ka (古都華) strawberries with crème d'ange.

anecdotes.text: The shop sits just south of the historic Daijoin Garden in the Naramachi district, marked by a 'NARAMACHI GARDEN' sign, with a shoes-off interior of raw wood and tatami plus a small garden-facing terrace.

Opening on essentially only Wednesdays and Thursdays, the limited schedule has helped build a devoted following among local 'gōrā' (shaved-ice enthusiasts), with about five varieties shown by photo at the counter each day.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: rurubu.jp/andmore/article/14214 confirms owner Okutani Miki as a former securities trader who prepared ~1 year and opened in 2019, the self-critical quality ethos, the Daijoin-adjacent 'NARAMACHI GARDEN' shoes-off tatami interior with terrace, the Wed/Thu-only schedule with ~5 daily varieties, and the signature bowls (salted coconut-pineapple with Nara konpeito from an Ansei-era confectioner, MAX Ginger, Koto-ka strawberry with crème d'ange).

positives.text: Syrups are made in-house from fruit and sugar, and the core product is shaved ice rather than wheat- or batter-based, so several bowls may suit avoiders of gluten if toppings are checked.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny shoes-off, garden-side shop run by one passionate owner with no English documented, so basic Japanese or a translation app helps for choosing among the daily bowls.

nara_latelier_cerisier.gf_detail: This is a French-style patisserie whose core products are wheat-based: cakes, galette bretonne, financiers and other baked goods all contain flour. No gluten-free items or accommodations are documented. Not suitable for celiacs. The shaved ice (kakigori) may use wheat-free syrups, but it is typically plated with cake/custard/baked elements, so cross-contact with wheat is very likely. Confirm directly before ordering if you have celiac disease.
nara_latelier_cerisier.vegan_detail: A pastry shop centered on butter, eggs, cream and dairy-rich custards (galette bretonne, financiers, fresh cakes, custard-and-cream shaved ice). No vegan items or plant-based options are documented. Not suitable for vegans.
nara_latelier_cerisier.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Fri 11:00–19:00 (L.O. 18:30); Sat, Sun & holidays 11:00–18:00 (L.O. 17:30); closes early when sold out. Closed Wed & Thu.
nara_latelier_cerisier.notes: [Mom & Pop] Latelier Cerisier opened in July 2023, founded by pastry chef Masayoshi Yamaguchi, who previously honed his craft as a pâtissier at the hotel The Hilltop Terrace Nara before striking out on his own just steps from Kintetsu Nara Station.

chef_bio.background: Latelier Cerisier opened in July 2023, founded by pastry chef Masayoshi Yamaguchi, who previously honed his craft as a pâtissier at the hotel The Hilltop Terrace Nara before striking out on his own just steps from Kintetsu Nara Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated aim is to make 'sweets that bring smiles and emotion,' pairing refined pâtisserie technique with careful, personal presentation.
chef_bio.specialty: French-style baked sweets and fresh cakes — signatures include galette bretonne and financiers — and, in the warmer months, elaborate dessert-style shaved ice (kakigori). The flagship 'Puin à la Mode' shaved ice is built like a composed dessert, layering caramel and custard sauce over baked custard, house-made berry ice, and pistachio and strawberry syrups that shift in flavor as you eat.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name 'cerisier' is French for cherry tree, and cherry-themed creations — including a shaved ice using two kinds of cherries with a vanilla anglaise sauce — are part of its identity.
To counter the chill of eating shaved ice, the shop offers guests complimentary roasted barley tea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: narakko.jp/latelier-cerisier confirms chef Masayoshi Yamaguchi (山口雅可), the July 2023 opening, his prior work at The Hilltop Terrace Nara, the Kintetsu-Nara-Station location, the 'smiles and emotion' aim, galette bretonne and financiers, the Puin à la Mode kakigori, and the complimentary roasted barley tea. nantokanko confirms the cerisier=cherry-tree name and cherry kakigori with vanilla anglaise.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood sweets shop where pointing at the display case and a few polite Japanese words go a long way; staff likely speak limited English, so a translation app helps for the kakigori menu.

nara_le_un_nipponia_hotel_nar.gf_detail: A French-based innovative restaurant; bread, flour, and dashi feature heavily in the cuisine, so it is not a dedicated or celiac-safe gluten-free venue. Allergies (which would include gluten/wheat) must be communicated at booking via the comments field or by phone at least 3 days in advance, as same-day accommodation is not possible. No documented dedicated gluten-free menu or fryer.
nara_le_un_nipponia_hotel_nar.vegan_detail: A French restaurant centered on Yamato pork, Yamato beef, Yamato chicken, fresh fish, and dairy; documented signature dishes are meat- and fish-based, so this is not a vegan or vegetarian destination. No vegan/vegetarian menu is documented. Dietary requests must be made at booking or by phone at least 3 days ahead; verify directly whether a plant-based course is possible.
nara_le_un_nipponia_hotel_nar.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:00), Dinner 17:30-22:00 (L.O. 20:00). Tuesday is dinner only (no lunch).
nara_le_un_nipponia_hotel_nar.notes: LE UN occupies a converted former sake brewery storehouse of the Toyosawa Sake Brewery within NIPPONIA HOTEL Nara Naramachi, set among the Edo-to-Taisho-era townscapes of Naramachi. The dining room is an intimate counter-style space carved out of a renovated traditional house.

roles: A Swiss-trained head chef leads the kitchen, described as bringing technique and refined sensibility.
chef_bio.background: LE UN occupies a converted former storehouse and residence of the Nara Toyosawa Sake Brewery within NIPPONIA HOTEL Nara Naramachi (rebranded 風のならまち / Kaze no Naramachi in 2026), set among the Edo-to-Taisho-era townscapes of Naramachi. The intimate counter-style dining room sits in what was once the building's earthen-floored doma.
chef_bio.philosophy: A local-production, local-consumption ethos: French technique used to draw out the true flavor of Nara's land and its traditional Yamato ingredients, with deliberate sake pairing.
chef_bio.specialty: Yamato French courses built on regional Nara ingredients: Yamato pork (served as confit with young spring vegetables), Yamato beef, Yamato chicken, and seasonal local vegetables and fruit, alongside dishes such as steamed fresh fish with zucchini and mint and conger eel carpione. Courses are designed to pair with sake from the affiliated Nara Toyosawa Sake Brewery.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant and hotel are housed in the renovated storehouse and former residence of the Meiji-era Nara Toyosawa Sake Brewery, with the counter dining room set in the building's former earthen-floored doma and courses paired to that brewery's sake.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tablecheck.com/naramachistay describes the Swiss-trained head chef, the Yamato pork/beef/chicken French with conger-eel carpione and steamed fish (zucchini/mint), and sake pairing from Toyosawa. kazenoheritage.jp confirms the property occupies the former Nara Toyosawa Sake Brewery residence (Meiji-founded), with counter dining in the former doma, and that the hotel rebranded to 風のならまち in June 2026.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Guests with allergies must inform the restaurant either in the comments field at the time of online booking or by phone at least 3 days in advance; due to ingredient preparation, same-day accommodation is not possible.

positives.text: The restaurant has a stated process for handling allergies when notified at least 3 days ahead of the reservation.

cultural_comfort.note: An English-language reservation site (TableCheck) and English menu descriptions exist, so a foreign student can book and dine comfortably, though this is a refined, higher-priced course restaurant rather than a casual spot.

nara_narameshi_itadakiya_sanj.gf_detail: No gluten-free program or labeling found on any page. This is a soy-sauce, sake, and tempura-heavy izakaya (fried items, grilled skewers with tare, simmered dishes), so wheat exposure is pervasive and it is not suitable for celiacs. No allergy or gluten information is published.
nara_narameshi_itadakiya_sanj.vegan_detail: A meat-and-fish izakaya centered on Yamato beef, pork, and chicken. It does feature Yamato heirloom vegetables and vegetable tempura, but no dedicated vegan menu exists and dashi/soy seasonings make most dishes non-vegan. A flexible vegan might find a few plain vegetable plates but should ask in advance; no vegan info is published.
nara_narameshi_itadakiya_sanj.hours_raw: Sources differ. Tabelog: Mon–Fri 17:00–24:00 (L.O. 23:30), Sat/Sun/holidays also lunch 11:30–14:00 plus 17:00–24:00; Gnavi: daily 17:00–24:00 (L.O. 23:30); one aggregator: Tue–Sun 17:00–23:00, closed Mon. Closed days reported inconsistently (open year-round on Tabelog vs Monday elsewhere).
nara_narameshi_itadakiya_sanj.notes: Itadakiya sits on Sanjo-dori, the historic approach toward Kasuga Taisha that has served pilgrims into Nara for centuries, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run by Ing, a Nara-based restaurant group, under the easygoing concept of a 'teishoku eatery where you

chef_bio.background: Itadakiya sits in Shimo-Sanjo-cho on Sanjo-dori, the historic approach toward Kasuga Taisha that has served pilgrims into Nara for centuries, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu and JR Nara stations. It is run by the Nara restaurant company Ing (株式会社イング), under the easygoing concept of a 'teishoku eatery where you can also drink' — comfortable enough for a quiet dinner or a group banquet.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing Nara's terroir — the kitchen selects vegetables daily and leans on nationally known Yamato heirloom varieties alongside local meats and sake, so a meal doubles as a tour of regional produce.
chef_bio.specialty: Creative 'Nara-meshi' cooking that puts local Yamato ingredients front and center: Yamato chicken and Yamato pork grilled as skewers over the robata, Yamato heirloom vegetables, and seasonal Nara produce chosen fresh each day. A signature is a green-tea-broth shabu hot pot with Yamato pork, paired with sake brought in from Nara-area breweries.

anecdotes.text: The house describes its food as creative cooking that makes the most of Nara ingredients, sourcing fresh local vegetables daily and building dishes around Yamato heirloom vegetables, Yamato chicken, and Yamato pork.
The kitchen's recommended course pairs the regional ingredients with two hours of free-flowing local sake, positioned as its confidence pick for both quantity and quality.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hotpepper.jp/strJ004004734 confirms the Yamato vegetable/pork/chicken focus, the green-tea-broth shabu-shabu with Yamato pork, local raw sake sourced from breweries, and 120-minute all-you-can-drink courses. ing-food.co.jp/shop/itadakiya-sanjo confirms the Shimo-Sanjo-cho location and operation by 株式会社イング.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free handling or fryer information is published; the menu is built around soy-sauce-based grilling, tempura, and simmered dishes, so wheat cross-contact should be assumed throughout.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Yakitori/grilled and simmered izakaya dishes typically use standard wheat-based soy sauce and tare; no gluten-free seasoning is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are prepared in a meat-and-fish kitchen and most use dashi or soy seasoning, so vegetable items are not reliably vegan; no separation is documented.

positives.text: An English menu is available, making it easier for a non-Japanese-speaking diner to identify and ask about ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: An English (and Chinese) menu is available and the place is used to both tourists and locals, so a foreign student can order comfortably even with limited Japanese.

nara_amenokaku_saryo.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. The signature items are wheat-based: house dorayaki (made from wheat-flour pancake batter) and freshly baked toast. Dango are rice-based but are served with mitarashi/sweet tare typically built on wheat-containing soy sauce, and there is no documented gluten-free or allergy program. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_amenokaku_saryo.vegan_detail: No documented vegan menu. Drinks include Yamato tea (matcha/sencha/houjicha), specialty coffee, and non-alcoholic mocktails, several of which may be plant-based, and lattes can presumably be made with plant milk if available, but this is unconfirmed. Sweets such as dorayaki and dango commonly contain egg/dairy and the tare may contain non-vegan elements, so a vegan visitor must ask item by item. No vegan claims are made by the shop.
nara_amenokaku_saryo.hours_raw: Sun-Thu: around midday to 17:00 (last order 16:30); Fri-Sat: around midday to 21:00 (last order 20:30), with Nara wine and alcoholic drinks served on Fri/Sat nights. Opening time was still being finalized at the time of the April 2026 report.
nara_amenokaku_saryo.notes: [Mom & Pop] 天迦久茶寮 opened in spring 2026 in a preserved merchant-house setting in Nara's historic Kitamachi quarter, on the old Kyoto highway just north of Kintetsu Nara Station near Todai-ji's Tegai Gate and Kaidan-in. It is the latest venue from the Nara coffee-and-tea group behind Amenokak

chef_bio.background: 天迦久茶寮 opened in spring 2026 in a preserved merchant-house setting in Nara's historic Kitamachi quarter, on the old Kyoto highway just north of Kintetsu Nara Station near Todai-ji's Tegai Gate and Kaidan-in. It is the latest venue from the Nara coffee-and-tea group behind Amenokaku Coffee, conceived as a grown-up retreat where guests slow down over carefully chosen drinks and sweets in a tranquil Japanese space.
chef_bio.philosophy: A tea house where adults can relax in a Japanese space, pairing locally rooted ingredients and craft with an unhurried, considered hospitality.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted specialty coffee and Yamato tea (matcha, sencha, houjicha) served alongside house-made wagashi and Western sweets, including the signature dorayaki and dango, plus freshly baked toast. Coffee and lattes are served in Akahada-yaki (Nara pottery) bowls with Nara motifs.

anecdotes.text: The interior spreads over two floors, with a modern ground floor and a tatami-mat second floor, while a small tsubo-niwa courtyard garden is tended by a landscaper who also maintains gardens at Kyoto's Taizo-in.
On Friday and Saturday evenings the cafe extends its hours and serves Nara wine and other alcoholic drinks, shifting from a daytime tea stop to an evening lounge.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-np.co.jp (Nara Shimbun, Apr 2026) confirms owner Ando Yui, the spring-2026 opening in Kitamachi by the Amenokaku Coffee group, self-roasted coffee and Yamato tea, house-made and Western sweets including dorayaki/dango and toast, Akahada-yaki serving bowls, the two-floor layout with a modern ground floor and tatami upper floor, the tsubo-niwa garden tended by a Taizo-in landscaper, and the extended Fri/Sat evening hours with Nara wine.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature dorayaki are made from wheat-flour batter and toast is baked on-site, so wheat is handled throughout the kitchen; no gluten-free preparation or separation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dango are typically served with mitarashi/sweet tare based on Japanese soy sauce, which usually contains wheat; the shop does not document wheat-free tare.

positives.text: Drinks lean toward tea and coffee, including Yamato tea and non-alcoholic mocktails, giving plant-based visitors some beverage options to ask about.

cultural_comfort.note: A calm, design-forward Japanese tea cafe in the quiet Kitamachi district; a foreign student would be comfortable but should expect a Japanese-language menu and may want a translation app or a Japanese-speaking companion to navigate the tea and sweets options.

nara_ohana_san_no_omusubi_yas.gf_detail: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. The single set meal includes miso soup (most miso/dashi seasonings are not declared gluten-free) plus grilled fish and side dishes; takeout items include tsukudani and seasoned kombu that typically use wheat-based soy sauce. While plain salted onigiri rice is naturally gluten-free, there is no gluten-free protocol, no documented separate prep, and the kitchen is not set up for celiac needs. No published allergen handling.
nara_ohana_san_no_omusubi_yas.vegan_detail: Not a vegetarian/vegan destination. The one set (はな結び定食) comes with grilled fish, and several onigiri fillings are fish-based (salmon, mentaiko). The morning miso soup is made with dashi (not specified as kombu-only), so it is likely not vegan. A vegan could potentially eat plain rice onigiri or homemade kombu onigiri à la carte, but this is not confirmed as animal-free and would need to be asked about in person. There is no documented vegan menu.
nara_ohana_san_no_omusubi_yas.hours_raw: Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat and occasionally Sun 7:30–10:00 (last order 9:30); takeout until around 12:00
nara_ohana_san_no_omusubi_yas.notes: [Mom & Pop] Originally from Wajima in Ishikawa Prefecture, the owner known as Ohana-san worked as a sales representative in Osaka before moving to Nara in 2013 out of deep affection for the city. She spent about seven years working at a traditional Japanese restaurant in the Gakuen-mae area,

chef_bio.background: Originally from Wajima in Ishikawa Prefecture, the owner known as Ohana-san worked as a sales representative in Osaka before moving to Nara in 2013 out of deep affection for the city. She spent about seven years working at a traditional Japanese restaurant in the Gakuen-mae area, then was invited to take over the unmanned bookstore Fuusenkazura, where she opened her onigiri shop in its kitchen in December 2020.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything is made carefully, one item at a time. The onigiri are formed gently so the grains loosen easily on the tongue, and the miso soup is made fresh each morning from freshly drawn dashi, aiming for a simple, gentle, refined plate.
chef_bio.specialty: A single set meal, the Hana-musubi teishoku (around 700 yen): two freshly hand-formed onigiri using Koshihikari rice from the Yamato Highlands, plus grilled fish, small side dishes, and miso soup. Fillings rotate among several options including homemade kombu, salmon, mentaiko, and pickled-greens combinations; takeout onigiri and homemade kombu/tsukudani are also sold.

anecdotes.text: She moved to Nara in 2013 simply because she loved the city so much, after a career in Osaka sales and seven years at a Japanese restaurant in Gakuen-mae.
She opened the onigiri shop in December 2020 inside the kitchen of the unmanned bookstore Fuusenkazura after being invited to become its proprietor.
Each onigiri is served freshly made to order, one at a time, with the second piece brought out after an interval so it is eaten warm.
The miso soup is made every morning from freshly taken dashi, and the set is praised as a simple yet gentle and refined one-plate breakfast.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nhmu.jp/people/41364 confirms the Wajima origin, Osaka sales career, 2013 move to Nara, ~7 years at a Gakuen-mae Japanese restaurant, and the Dec 2020 opening inside the unmanned bookstore Fuusenkazura. narakko.jp/ohanasan confirms the single Hana-musubi teishoku (¥700) with two Yamato-Highlands Koshihikari onigiri, grilled fish, sides and fresh-daily-dashi miso soup, plus the one-at-a-time hand-forming and takeout kombu.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Takeout offerings include homemade kombu and tsukudani, which are typically simmered in wheat-based soy sauce; soy sauce content is not declared gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The set comes with grilled fish and the miso soup is made with morning dashi (not specified as kombu-only), so vegan separation is not assured.

positives.text: Rice is the focus: Koshihikari from the Yamato Highlands, with onigiri formed gently to order, so plain salted or kombu onigiri may be requestable à la carte.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny solo-run morning counter inside a Japanese bookstore where little to no English is likely, so a few Japanese phrases and patience will make for a smooth, warm visit.

nara_omusubi_dokoro_wagaya.gf_detail: Plain rice balls (especially the shio-musubi / salted onigiri) are naturally based on rice, but this is not a gluten-free destination and there is no documented allergen handling. The signature 一汁三菜 set is built around miso soup and assorted side dishes; miso typically contains barley or wheat, the soup uses dashi, and side dishes and certain fillings can contain wheat-based soy sauce. A celiac traveler would need to ask in detail, and no dedicated gluten-free practices are documented.
nara_omusubi_dokoro_wagaya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan destination. Several fillings are animal-based (salmon, etc.) and the popular sets include miso soup that almost certainly uses fish dashi, plus a rolled-omelet (dashimaki) option made with egg. A few items such as the plain salted rice ball or umboshi (plum) onigiri may be plant-based, but vegan suitability is not documented and would need to be confirmed directly.
nara_omusubi_dokoro_wagaya.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, hand-made-onigiri shop that opened in autumn 2023 on Nara's retro Funabashi shopping street. It is run single-handedly by a young proprietor who first opened the shop while still a fourth-year university student and has since graduated holding childcare and kindergarten-

chef_bio.background: A small, hand-made-onigiri shop that opened in autumn 2023 on Nara's retro Funabashi shopping street. It is run single-handedly by a young proprietor who first opened the shop while still a university student and has since graduated holding childcare and kindergarten-teaching qualifications, with an aspiration to one day work in child- and family-support services. The shop name Wagaya draws on the owner's own name and carries the wish that guests will treat the place like their own home.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner chose this calm corner of the old shopping street specifically to give guests a peaceful, restful experience, reflecting the neighborhood spirit of being kind to both heart and body; a small raised seating area stocked with toys and picture books welcomes families with young children.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-formed rice balls made from carefully chosen Hokkaido-grown Yumepirika rice, prized for its natural sweetness and for keeping its flavor even after it cools. The signature 一汁三菜 (one-soup, three-side) set pairs two rice balls of your choice with a miso soup and three small side dishes, and there is an equally popular set that swaps in a fluffy rolled-omelet (dashimaki). Roughly ten regular fillings rotate with the seasons, alongside a simple salted rice ball.

anecdotes.text: The owner tasted many rice varieties before settling on Hokkaido Yumepirika because its grains stay sweet and flavorful even once cooled, making it ideal for both dine-in and takeout rice balls.
Within months of opening, 30 to 40 percent of customers had become repeat visitors, a sign of how the cozy, home-like atmosphere resonated with locals.
The shop opened while its proprietor was still a university student, who has since graduated with childcare and kindergarten-teaching licenses and hopes to move into child and family support work.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: narakko.jp/wagaya confirms the autumn-2023 Funabashi-shopping-street opening, the student-owner who later earned childcare/kindergarten licenses, the Wagaya name (owner's name + home wish), Hokkaido Yumepirika rice, the 一汁三菜 and dashimaki sets with ~10 fillings, the 30-40% repeat-customer rate, and the kids' toy/picture-book seating area. goguynet corroborates the Yumepirika choice for staying sweet when cooled.

positives.text: The owner is selective about ingredients, choosing a specific Hokkaido rice variety along with particular salt and miso, and works alone, so it is feasible to ask directly about how a dish is made.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, warm solo-run neighborhood shop where ordering is simple but interaction is in Japanese, so a few basic phrases will help a foreign student feel at ease.

nara_washokoro_yoshino.gf_detail: A traditional Japanese kaiseki restaurant. Course menus rely heavily on soy sauce and dashi (typically fish-based), and dishes commonly include wheat-containing seasonings and items, so it is not a celiac-safe environment without direct confirmation. The hotel publishes an allergen-information document, so it is best to call ahead (0742-35-5819) and discuss gluten needs in advance.
nara_washokoro_yoshino.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore kaiseki restaurant; most courses feature fish, fish-based dashi, and other animal products. While Yamato/Nara vegetables and Nara-pickle (奈良漬) feature in the cooking, no documented vegan menu exists. Vegetarian/vegan needs should be arranged in advance by phone, ideally when reserving.
nara_washokoro_yoshino.notes: A full Japanese-cuisine dining room serving seasonal washoku and kaiseki built around carefully chosen ingredients. The kitchen leans into the local larder, featuring Yamato/Nara vegetables, Nara-pickle (nara-zuke), and the regional rice and produce that define Nara's table.

chef_bio.origin: Central Nara, on the third floor of Hotel Nikko Nara, directly connected to the west exit of JR Nara Station.
chef_bio.background: A full Japanese-cuisine dining room serving seasonal washoku and kaiseki-style courses built around carefully chosen ingredients, leaning into the regional Nara larder and local produce that define the area's table.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house describes its cooking as dishes woven from carefully examined, dependable ingredients and a spirit of hospitality that spares no effort (吟味した確かな食材と、手間を惜しまないおもてなしの心で綴る逸品).
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal kaiseki and course menus that change with the four seasons, paired with a curated flight of Nara local sake — the '奈良地酒めぐり' offered from a three-type tasting up to a six-type selection, a nod to Nara being regarded as a birthplace of sake brewing.

anecdotes.text: Diners come to experience the four seasons through Japanese cuisine (四季折々の味), with a head-chef-curated Nara local-sake tasting line-up.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ホテル日航奈良3階（JR奈良駅西口直結）の和食処よしの。四季折々の会席・和食を「吟味した確かな食材と、手間を惜しまないおもてなしの心で綴る逸品」として提供。奈良地酒めぐり（3種〜6種）を用意。

staff_allergy_handling.text: The hotel provides an allergen-information document, indicating that allergy inquiries are handled, though specific gluten/vegan handling details were not published.

cultural_comfort.note: As a polished hotel restaurant directly connected to JR Nara Station, staff are used to guests and reservations can be made online, though a few words of Japanese and an advance call about any dietary needs will make the visit smoother.

nara_gen_soba.gf_detail: Gen makes both its seiro/zaru and inaka soba as jūwari (100% buckwheat) with no wheat binder: the venue's own coverage states 「毎朝石臼で自家製粉、つなぎを使わない十割そば」— buckwheat stone-ground in-house each morning and cut ultra-thin. That makes the noodle itself celiac-plausible, but the tsuyu is a kombu/shiitake/bonito dashi cut with soy sauce (wheat unless tamari), so ask specifically for a wheat-free dip. Critically, each order is boiled individually rather than in one batch, which is favorable — but a fully dedicated GF boiling-water/pot is unconfirmed, and any tempura side shares oil. Confirm tamari-based tsuyu and dedicated water before ordering.
nara_gen_soba.vegan_detail: Not a vegan kitchen. The dipping dashi contains bonito, so standard seiro/zaru is not vegan. The mizu-soba (梅たたき水蕎麦) is eaten with spring water and ume rather than dashi tsuyu, so a plant-based bowl may be possible — confirm no bonito or dashi in the ume/garnish.
nara_gen_soba.hours_raw: Tue–Fri 11:30–13:30 (LO 13:00) & 18:00–21:00 (18:00 entry, reservation); Sat 11:30–13:30; closed Sun & Mon
nara_gen_soba.notes: [GF] Michelin-listed, Tabelog-100 jūwari soba shop where both the seiro and inaka soba are 100% buckwheat with no wheat binder, boiled to order. The noodle is celiac-plausible but the soy-based tsuyu and shared boiling water are the risk — go at lunch, ask for tamari tsuyu and dedicated water, and skip any tempura. Reservation effectively required (daily servings capped), cash only.

chef_bio.background: Gen is run by owner-chef Hiroyuki Shimazaki in a quiet house in Naramachi's Fukuchiin-cho. Before soba, Shimazaki worked as a craftsman shaving reeds for woodwind instruments, precision work measured at the micron level, and he carries that exactness into milling and cutting. He stone-grinds only the day's portion of buckwheat each morning and cuts the jūwari noodles ultra-thin so they cook quickly without a binder. The shop appears repeatedly in the Michelin guide and on Tabelog's soba-100 list.
chef_bio.philosophy: Freshly self-milled buckwheat, no tsunagi (wheat binder), noodles cut thin and boiled by the portion for peak aroma.
chef_bio.specialty: Jūwari seiro and inaka (hull-in) soba; mizu-soba with ume

anecdotes.text: Shimazaki notes jūwari soba stretches easily, so he cuts it thin and boils each order individually rather than in a batch (十割蕎麦は伸びやすいんです。蕎麦を一人前ずつ湯がきたいので).
He came to soba from making micron-precise reeds for woodwind instruments, and still crafts reeds between restaurant duties.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: JR Central いざいざ奈良, 日本蕎麦保存会 (nihon-soba.jp) and Tabelog all describe Gen as a hand-milled 100% buckwheat, no-binder shop that boils each order individually; JR Central quotes owner Shimazaki and his instrument-reed background.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Noodles are boiled individually per order rather than in a shared batch, which reduces (but does not eliminate) noodle-to-noodle cross-contact; a fully dedicated GF pot/water is unconfirmed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsuyu is a kombu/shiitake/bonito dashi finished with soy sauce; standard soy sauce contains wheat, so a tamari-based dip must be requested and is unconfirmed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dipping dashi contains bonito; mizu-soba (water + ume) is the only plausibly plant-based option and should be confirmed.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No published gluten-free or allergen policy; celiac accommodation (tamari, dedicated water) is unverified and must be arranged directly.

positives.text: Both soba types are jūwari (100% buckwheat) with no wheat binder, hand-milled fresh each morning.
Each portion is boiled to order rather than in a shared batch.

nara_happysmile_komeko.gf_detail: [Adversarial GF review 2026-08-19: high→options. I tried to find a second genuinely independent source and could not: both cited write-ups (bagel-atsume and nara.goguynet) are November 2025 opening announcements reprinting the shop's own launch copy, there is no FindMeGlutenFree/HappyCow/celiac corroboration anywhere, and when I fetched the shop's only official channel (Instagram, which the record uses as its website) the visible bio does not surface an explicit グルテンフリー or 米粉100% statement at all. Against that sits a concrete unresolved wheat vector the record itself flagged and nobody has closed: the 焦がしみたらし×チーズ bagel, since mitarashi glaze is soy-sauce based and default Japanese soy sauce is wheat; the bacon epi is a second unverified processed-meat vector. This is a two-days-a-week micro-bakery that opened nine months ago and also runs bread classes on the same premises, with zero published allergen handling. One source cannot support high — capped at options.] Dedicated 100% rice-flour bagel bakery — the shop bakes no wheat at all. Own claim: 「国産米粉100％を使用した無添加でグルテンフリーのもちもち食感が特徴」 (100% domestic rice flour, additive-free, gluten-free, chewy texture). Because every product is 米粉-based there is no wheat flour on premises, but this is a tiny home-scale operation that opened 7 Nov 2025 and also runs rice-flour bread classes; there is no published celiac cross-contact protocol, so highly-sensitive coeliacs should confirm mix-in ingredients (some bagels use cheese, bacon or chocolate) and any shared equipment.
nara_happysmile_komeko.vegan_detail: Bagels are 米粉 (rice flour) and additive-free, so plainer varieties (プレーン, 玄米ブレンド, 黒糖栗, ほうじ茶あんこ, ごまあんこ) may be plant-based, but several flavors contain animal products — チーズ (cheese), ベーコンエピ (bacon), ピーナッツバター, and ホワイトチョコ / クランベリーチョコ. No explicit vegan labelling; confirm dairy/egg per flavor with the shop.
nara_happysmile_komeko.hours_raw: Tue & Sun from 12:00 (until sold out). New shop opened November 7, 2025; small operation, so confirm days/hours.
nara_happysmile_komeko.notes: [GF-dedicated] 100% rice-flour bagel bakery in Kidera-cho (just south of Naramachi), opened 7 Nov 2025. No wheat is baked, so bagels are inherently gluten-free, but it's a very new micro-bakery with tiny hours (currently Tue & Sun from 12:00) and no formal celiac protocol — check the Instagram for the week's opening days and sold-out status before going, and confirm mix-in ingredients if extremely sensitive. One parking space at the rear; coin parking nearby.

chef_bio.background: HAPPY SMILE KOMEKO opened on 7 November 2025 in Nara's Kidera-cho by an owner who is a former firefighter and emergency-medical technician (元消防士・救急救命士). Local press reports the owner discovered rice-flour bread in October 2024 and started 'from zero,' building the business over about a year before opening. The shop shares an address with the yakigashi maker 'taruha' and sits in the quiet Kidera-cho district south of Naramachi near a recently relocated neighbor, with one on-site parking space. Alongside bagel sales the owner offers rice-flour bread-making classes.
chef_bio.philosophy: Store motto: 「米粉パンでハッピー×スマイルを届けること」 — to deliver happiness and smiles through rice-flour bread.
chef_bio.specialty: Additive-free, 100% domestic rice-flour (国産米粉100%) chewy bagels.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a former firefighter/paramedic (元消防士・救急救命士) who left to pursue rice-flour baking after discovering it in October 2024.

nara_udon_ichigo_ichie.notes: [Mom & Pop · udon] A tiny (~10-seat) hand-made udon counter that opened May 2026 directly across from Kintetsu Nara Station (Exit 1), on Noborioji-dōri toward Nara Park — in the former site of a kushiya.
